children.note: Pouring a bucket of water with a little soap over a square metre drives mole crickets to the surface within minutes, a simple way to see how many there are.
Molluscs that rasp holes in seedlings, leaves and tubers, mainly in cool, damp weather and under heavy mulch or weeds.
Ragged holes in leaves, seedlings eaten to the stalk overnight and shiny slime trails. Go out with a torch after dark to see them feeding.

manas.q: What shiny sign shows that slugs or snails have been feeding?

children.note: Lissachatina (Achatina) fulica is a big invasive snail in Kenya, India and many tropical islands. It eats many crops and should be hand-collected and destroyed; it can carry a rat lungworm, so wear gloves.
Boards, upturned pots or cabbage leaves give them a daytime hiding place; check and collect each morning. Shallow traps of beer or yeast water also draw slugs in.
Ferric phosphate slug pellets are permitted in organic farming in many standards and break down to iron and phosphate in soil. Metaldehyde pellets are not allowed in organic.

manas.q: Which type of slug pellet is accepted in organic farming?

children.note: Burrowing rodents eat seed, roots and tubers. In East Africa mole rats (Tachyoryctes) and field rats are common.
Fresh soil mounds without an open hole (mole rats), rows of dug-up seed, gnawed tubers and wilting plants with roots chewed off.
Traps set in the runs, clean field edges with short grass, perches and nest boxes for owls and hawks, and cats or dogs around stores. Poison baits are not allowed under organic standards.
Count soil pests before planting so you know whether action is needed. Exact thresholds depend on crop and region, so use them as a guide only.
Dig several pits about 30 × 30 cm and 20–30 cm deep across the field, sieve or break the soil and count grubs, cutworms and wireworms. Record the numbers each season.

manas.q: How big is a typical soil sampling pit for counting grubs?

children.note: Cutworms, slugs and mole crickets are active at night. A short walk at first light finds fresh damage and the pests before they hide.
Soil pests are patchy. Marking damaged spots shows where to treat next season instead of the whole field.
Insect-killing fungi and nematodes live naturally in soil and can be added as products. They act slowly and need moisture, but suit organic systems well.

Metarhizium anisopliae and related species are green-spored soil fungi that infect insects through the skin. They are among the best-tested biological agents against white grubs, wireworms and some termites.

manas.q: How does Metarhizium get into an insect?

children.note: Beauveria bassiana is a white-spored relative used mainly against insects above ground, but also against some soil beetles and weevils. It needs humid conditions to sporulate.
Mix spore powder with well-made compost or FYM and apply in the planting furrow or planting hole, then water. Keep away from chemical fungicides and strong sun, and repeat each season.
Both fungi can live in crop roots as harmless endophytes after a soil drench, which may give longer-lasting protection. Field benefit varies and is still being studied.
Termites groom and isolate infected nestmates, so fungal spores rarely destroy a whole colony. Fungi are best seen as part of termite management, not a cure.

manas.q: Why do insect-killing fungi rarely wipe out termite colonies?

children.note: Microscopic worms (Steinernema, Heterorhabditis) that enter grubs, cutworms and weevil larvae and release bacteria that kill the host in a few days. They then multiply inside and spread to new hosts.

manas.q: Which two nematode genera are used to kill soil insects?

children.note: Apply in the evening or on cloudy days to moist soil, water in, and keep moist for two weeks. They die in sun, heat and dry soil, and must be used before the expiry date.
Plant-based materials worked into soil can deter or slow soil pests. Effects are usually partial and depend on dose and soil life.

The residue left after pressing neem seed for oil. Mixed into soil at planting it acts as an organic fertiliser and its limonoids (such as azadirachtin) deter and disrupt grubs, termites and nematodes. Widely used in India.

manas.q: What is neem cake and how does it act against soil pests?

children.note: A traditional dusting around seedlings against cutworms, termites and slugs. Fresh ash is caustic and drying, but it washes out with rain, raises soil pH, and good trial evidence is scarce. Use small amounts only.

manas.q: What are two drawbacks of wood ash as a pest treatment?

children.note: Leaves of Tithonia, Tephrosia, castor or Lantana are traditionally added to planting holes against termites. Most evidence is from farmer experience and small trials, so test on a small area first.
Field practices are the base of organic soil-pest control, but each has costs as well as benefits.

Ploughing in the dry season brings grubs and pupae to the surface where sun and birds kill them. But frequent deep tillage harms earthworms, soil structure and organic matter, so use it as a targeted tool, not every year.

manas.q: What is the trade-off of ploughing to expose white grubs?

children.note: Flooding a field for a few days drowns cutworms, mole crickets and grubs, and is natural in paddy rice. In rain-fed farming it is rarely possible, and it can damage soil structure.
Mulch gives termites something to eat besides the crop and builds soil, but it also shelters slugs, snails and millipedes. Keep mulch on the field but pull it back a hand-width from young stems.

manas.q: Why can mulch reduce termite attack on the crop itself?

children.note: Rotating away from grass, cereals and potatoes for a year or two, for example into legumes or brassicas, breaks the food supply of grubs and wireworms.
Timely planting, good soil moisture and balanced nutrition help plants outgrow root damage. Termite damage to maize is clearly worse in drought-stressed fields.
Apply manure only after it is fully composted. Hot composting also kills grub and cutworm stages that may be in the heap.
Natural predators and simple traps keep soil pest numbers down at low cost.
Egrets, crows, hornbills and starlings follow ploughing and eat grubs and cutworms. Perches and trees on field edges help them stay.
Chickens let onto a field after harvest or before planting scratch out grubs and cutworms; ducks are very good at eating slugs and snails. Keep them off young crops.

manas.q: Which poultry is especially good at eating slugs and snails?

children.note: Ground beetles, rove beetles, centipedes and ants feed on soil pest eggs and larvae. Permanent grassy strips and reduced spraying keep them in the field.
Moist bran mixed with a little molasses and spread at dusk draws cutworms out; they can be collected at night. Commercial Bt or nematode baits use the same idea.
Traditional East African practice often targets the mound and its queen rather than the termites in the field.

Digging out a Macrotermes mound and removing the queen can stop that colony, and farmers in Kenya and Uganda do this. It is heavy work, colonies of some species can re-queen, and other colonies nearby keep foraging.

manas.q: What are two limits of removing the termite queen?

children.note: Mound soil is richer in clay and nutrients and is used for bricks and as fertiliser. Removing only mounds close to young trees and high-value crops keeps the benefits.
Plant seedlings with compost, water well, mulch with dry grass away from the stem, and avoid planting into wood debris. Healthy, unstressed seedlings are attacked less.
Some common practices are illegal in organic farming or harmful to people and soil.
Chlorpyrifos, fipronil, imidacloprid and similar soil insecticides and seed dressings are not allowed in organic certification, and many are banned or restricted in Kenya, India and the EU.

manas.q: Are imidacloprid seed dressings allowed in organic farming?

children.note: Pouring used engine oil, kerosene or diesel into mounds or planting holes poisons soil and water and is never organic.
Dig before acting. Earthworms, beetles and many termites in a healthy soil are helpers, and killing them hurts soil fertility.
Short videos from research, extension and farmer-to-farmer channels.
Kenya’s Agroecology Hub — farmers in western Kenya show how they cut termite damage without chemicals.
University of Wisconsin IPM — identifying grubs, wireworms, seedcorn maggot and cutworms early in the season.
Virginia Tech Eastern Shore AREC — wireworm biology and management in potatoes.
University of Florida entomology — the fly, the wasp and the nematode used against mole crickets.
An experienced gardener shows a simple pot trap for slugs and snails.
Reliable starting points for deeper study.
Free East African plant-health guide with pages on termites, white grubs, cutworms and organic control.
How insect-killing nematodes and their bacteria work.
Biology and uses of the green muscardine fungus.
Termite biology, castes and ecology.

nodeData.note: Insects, moulds and aflatoxin that attack grain and beans after harvest, and the organic ways to stop them: harvest and drying, airtight storage, inert dusts, botanicals, clean stores and monitoring.

children.note: After months of work in the field, a large share of grain can be lost in the store to insects, moulds and rodents. Good storage protects food, income and health.
A major review reports that cereal losses in storage can reach 50–60% where storage is poor, and that improved storage methods can cut losses to as little as 1–2%.

manas.q: How low can improved storage bring cereal storage losses?

children.note: Insect damage lowers weight, germination and market price, and holes made by insects let moulds in, raising the risk of aflatoxin.
Organic standards do not allow synthetic storage insecticides or chemical fumigants, so the system relies on drying, cleaning, airtight storage, inert dusts and botanicals.

manas.q: What does organic grain storage rely on instead of synthetic insecticides?

children.note: Sitophilus zeamais (maize weevil) and S. oryzae (rice weevil) are the most widespread storage pests of maize, sorghum, rice and wheat in the tropics.
Small dark-brown beetles, about 3–4 mm long, with a long snout and often four faint orange spots on the wing cases. The two species look almost the same.

manas.q: What body feature identifies a weevil?

children.note: The female chews a hole, lays one egg inside the kernel and seals it. The larva eats and pupates inside, so infested grain looks clean until adults emerge.
Neat round exit holes in kernels, fine flour dust, grain that feels warm, and kernels that float in water because they are hollow.

manas.q: Why do weevil-infested kernels float in water?

children.note: Weevils fly from old stores to maturing maize in the field, especially where husk cover is poor. Late harvest gives them more time to settle in.
Prostephanus truncatus, a small bostrichid beetle native to Mexico and Central America, is the most destructive pest of farm-stored maize and dried cassava in East and West Africa.
It was accidentally introduced to Tanzania in the late 1970s and spread through much of sub-Saharan Africa, including Kenya. Models show it could still spread to new areas.

manas.q: Where did the larger grain borer first arrive in Africa?

children.note: A cylindrical dark-brown beetle about 3–4 mm long whose head is tucked under the thorax, so no snout is visible from above. It is a borer, not a weevil.
Adults tunnel from grain to grain and leave large piles of fine grain dust. They also bore into dried cassava chips, wooden store beams and sacks, and can destroy cob maize in a few months.

manas.q: What does LGB leave behind that weevils usually do not?

children.topic: Store shelled, not on the cob
children.note: LGB does best on maize kept on the cob, especially with husks. Shelling, drying well and storing in airtight containers greatly reduces damage.

A small predatory beetle from Central America, Teretrius nigrescens, was released in several African countries from the 1990s and feeds on LGB in the wild. It lowers outbreaks but does not protect a single store on its own.
Traps baited with the LGB aggregation pheromone show when beetles are flying in an area, so farmers know when to harvest promptly and seal stores.
Bruchids (bean weevils) such as Acanthoscelides obtectus on common beans and Callosobruchus maculatus and C. chinensis on cowpea, grams and pigeon pea.
Small round "windows" on seeds where larvae inside are close to the surface, then neat exit holes, powder and small oval beetles running in the store.

manas.q: What are the round "windows" on stored beans?

children.note: Eggs are often laid on drying pods before harvest, so newly harvested beans can already be infested. Fast harvest and threshing help.
Mixing beans or cowpeas with a small amount of vegetable oil coats the seed so eggs and young larvae suffocate. This is a long-standing household method for seed and food beans.
Moth larvae feed on grain and flour, mainly in the top layer of a store.
Sitotroga cerealella. Larvae develop inside maize, rice, sorghum and wheat kernels; adults leave small round holes, often with a thin flap. Infestation can begin in the field.

manas.q: Which storage moth develops inside whole kernels?

children.note: Plodia interpunctella. Larvae spin silk webbing through flour, broken grain, dried fruit and nuts. A pest of processed food in homes and shops worldwide.

manas.q: What sign typically shows Indian meal moth?

children.note: Most moth damage is in the upper 30 cm of grain in bulk. Airtight containers, fine-mesh covers and stirring the top layer limit them.
Several more beetles attack stored grain and flour.

children.topic: Flour beetles and lesser grain borer
children.note: Red flour beetle (Tribolium castaneum) feeds on broken grain and flour; lesser grain borer (Rhyzopertha dominica) bores whole grains like a small LGB. Both follow primary pests.
Trogoderma granarium hairy larvae devastate grain in hot, dry regions including India. Many countries list it as a quarantine pest, so report suspected finds.
Moulds such as Aspergillus, Fusarium and Penicillium grow on damp or damaged grain. Some produce mycotoxins; aflatoxins are the most dangerous.
A group of poisons made mainly by Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus on maize, groundnuts, sorghum and other crops. Aflatoxin B1 is the most potent.

manas.q: Which two fungi mainly produce aflatoxins?

children.note: High doses cause acute liver failure (aflatoxicosis); long-term low exposure is linked to liver cancer and weakened immunity. Animals fed contaminated feed grow poorly and dairy cows pass a form (M1) into milk.
In 2004 one of the largest known aflatoxicosis outbreaks hit eastern and central Kenya, with 317 cases and 125 deaths, traced to contaminated home-grown maize.

manas.q: How many deaths did Kenya’s 2004 aflatoxin outbreak cause?

children.note: Kenya has had repeated outbreaks, especially in the drier eastern counties such as Makueni and Kitui, where a toxic strain type of A. flavus is common.
Aflatoxin has no colour, smell or taste in grain, and normal cooking does not destroy it. Visible mould is a warning, but clean-looking grain can still be contaminated.

manas.q: Does cooking destroy aflatoxin?

children.note: Drought and heat stress during grain fill, insect damage, late harvest, drying on bare ground, rain on harvested crop and storage above safe moisture.
Rapid test kits and labs measure aflatoxin in parts per billion. Buyers, millers and feed makers in Kenya increasingly test lots, and contaminated grain must not be sold for food or feed.
Aflasafe products use native strains of Aspergillus flavus that cannot make aflatoxin to crowd out the toxic strains in the field.

The non-toxic strains are coated on sterile sorghum grain and spread on the soil before the crop flowers. They grow, sporulate and take over the niche on the crop, leaving less room for toxin-producing strains.

manas.q: How do atoxigenic A. flavus strains reduce aflatoxin?

children.note: Reviews of African trials report that atoxigenic biocontrol reduces aflatoxin in maize and groundnut by about 70–90%.

manas.q: By how much does atoxigenic biocontrol typically cut aflatoxin?

children.note: Each product is made from strains native to that country. Versions have been registered in Kenya, Nigeria, Senegal and The Gambia, among others; the Kenyan one was developed with KALRO.
It works in the field, not in a store: grain must still be dried and stored well. Organic farmers should confirm with their certifier whether a given product is permitted.
Most storage problems are decided at harvest. Dry, clean, undamaged grain stores well; damp grain spoils whatever the container.
Harvest as soon as the crop is mature and dry enough. Leaving maize in the field for weeks invites weevils, LGB, moulds and termites.
Dry cobs or grain on tarpaulins, mats, raised cribs or cement floors, not on the ground, where soil carries Aspergillus spores and moisture.

manas.q: Why should grain never be dried on bare soil?

children.note: Grain should be dried to about 13% moisture before storage to keep insects and moulds slow. Moisture meters give a reading; simpler tests give a yes/no.

manas.q: To about what moisture should grain be dried before storage?

children.note: Shake a little dry salt with grain in a clean, dry glass bottle for a few minutes. If salt sticks to the glass, the grain is still too wet to store.

manas.q: What does it mean if salt sticks to the bottle in the salt test?

children.note: Remove mouldy, shrivelled, broken and insect-damaged cobs and kernels; they carry most of the aflatoxin and insects. Feed them to nobody.
Hermetic (airtight) storage starves insects of oxygen without chemicals. PICS bags, developed at Purdue University, are the best-known type in Africa and Asia.
Inside a sealed bag, insects and grain use up oxygen and build up carbon dioxide. Insects stop feeding, stop breeding and die, so damage stays very low.

manas.q: What kills insects inside a hermetic bag?

children.note: Two inner liners of thick polyethylene sit inside an outer woven polypropylene bag. Each liner is twisted, folded and tied separately to make the seal airtight.

manas.q: How many layers does a PICS bag have?

children.note: Airtight bags hold moisture in. Grain stored too damp can still go mouldy, and opening bags often lets oxygen back in and raises fungal growth and aflatoxin risk.

links.label: 📄 J Stored Prod Res 2016 (opening PICS bags)

children.note: A survey of 613 farmers in eastern Kenya found hermetic storage use rose from about 54% in 2015 to 91% in 2017, with PICS the most used and storage judged profitable.
Store bags off the floor, away from rats and sharp objects, and check liners for holes before reuse. A hole as small as a pin lets air in and the seal fails.
Airtight galvanised-steel silos built by trained local artisans, promoted by CIMMYT and others for farm households in Africa and Central America.
When sealed, a silo is hermetic like a PICS bag and also keeps out rats and birds. Sizes range from a few hundred kilograms to a few tonnes.
Before sealing, a lit candle placed on top of the grain burns off part of the oxygen; it goes out when oxygen is low. The lid is then sealed with rubber or grease.

manas.q: Why do farmers put a burning candle in a metal silo before sealing?

children.note: They cost more than bags at the start but can last many years, so cost per year is often low. Keep them in the shade to avoid heating and condensation.
Dusts that kill insects physically, not chemically. Many are permitted in organic storage.
A fine powder of fossil algae shells. It scratches and absorbs the waxy outer layer of insects, so they lose water and die. Grain is usually treated at low rates of around 1 g per kg.

manas.q: How does diatomaceous earth kill stored-grain insects?

children.note: DE kills faster at higher temperature and lower humidity, so it suits dry grain in warm stores. In very humid conditions it works more slowly.

links.label: 📄 J Econ Entomol 2000 (DE vs temperature & RH)

children.note: A traditional method: mixing clean, sieved wood ash or fine sand with grain fills the spaces between kernels and hinders insects. It works best in small, full containers.
Wear a dust mask when mixing; use food-grade amorphous DE, not the crystalline pool-filter type. Sieve or wash grain before milling.
Plant materials mixed with grain or used to line stores repel or kill storage insects. Results are usually partial and fade with time.
Dried neem leaves or neem seed powder mixed with grain or seed deter weevils and bruchids. A long-standing practice in India and East Africa.

manas.q: Which tree’s leaves and seed powder are a traditional grain protectant?

children.note: Leaves of this "fish-bean" shrub are dried and mixed with stored beans and maize in East and Southern Africa. They contain rotenoids, which are toxic: use for seed or with care, and never near fish ponds.
Dried chilli or black pepper powder repels insects and is used with beans and grain in many homes. Taste and handling need care.
Lantana or eucalyptus leaves layered with stored maize are reported to discourage LGB and weevils, as part of a wider storage plan.
Purified rotenone is no longer permitted in EU organic farming. Check your certifier’s rules before using any botanical product beyond home use.
Most new infestations come from leftover grain and dirty stores.
Sweep out old grain, dust and husks, repair cracks and burn or bury the sweepings. Old stores can carry LGB and weevils waiting for new grain.

manas.q: Where do new storage infestations usually come from?

children.note: Dip used sacks in boiling water or sun them well before reuse to kill hidden eggs and larvae.
Stack bags on pallets off the floor and away from walls, keep new grain away from old, and keep the store cool, dry and rat-proof.
Check stored grain regularly so problems are caught early.
Take samples from the top, middle and sides, sieve and count insects, and look for dust, webbing, warmth, caking or a musty smell.
Hot spots, damp lumps or a sour, mouldy smell show moisture or insect activity. Spread, re-dry and sort the grain at once.
Pheromone traps catch LGB and moths; probe and pitfall traps show beetles in bulk grain. They warn early, before damage is visible.
Common shortcuts that are illegal in organic farming or dangerous.

children.topic: No synthetic grain dusts or fumigants
children.note: Synthetic insecticide dusts and phosphine fumigation tablets are not allowed under organic standards. Phosphine is also highly poisonous to people when misused in homes.

manas.q: Is phosphine fumigation allowed in organic storage?

children.note: Never mix mouldy grain with good grain to sell or feed it; the toxin remains and spreads to the whole lot.
Videos from research institutes and farmer-training organisations.
Access Agriculture — a farmer-to-farmer guide to drying, cleaning and storing maize.
Access Agriculture — how aflatoxin develops after harvest and how to prevent it.

children.topic: ▶ The story of aflatoxin and Aflasafe
children.note: IITA — how native non-toxic Aspergillus strains protect crops in Africa.
Purdue PICS programme — filling and tying the triple-layer bag correctly.
Scientific Animations Without Borders (SAWBO) — the salt-in-a-bottle test step by step.
CIMMYT — how farm households use metal silos to protect grain.
Reliable starting points for deeper study.
Review of storage losses and hermetic technologies for developing countries.
Toxins 2019 review of atoxigenic Aspergillus biocontrol: benefits and limits.
Biology, spread and management of Prostephanus truncatus.
East African guide with pages on storage pests and safe storage.

nodeData.note: Weeds are managed, not eradicated, on an organic farm. The aim is to stop them hurting yield during the crop's sensitive window and to shrink the weed seed bank year by year — using prevention, smart timing, soil cover, tools and living plants instead of synthetic herbicides.

children.note: Weeds compete with crops for light, water and nutrients, and some host pests and diseases. But they also bring real benefits, so the goal is control, not a bare field.
Weeds take water, nitrogen and light, especially when the crop is young. Losses are often bigger on poor, dry soils where every resource counts.

manas.q: What do weeds compete with crops for?

children.note: Some weeds carry viruses, nematodes or insects that move onto crops; e.g. nightshade-family weeds can host pests of tomato and potato.
They cover bare soil against erosion, feed pollinators and natural enemies with flowers, and can be cut for mulch, fodder or compost.

manas.q: Name three benefits weeds can give a farm.

children.note: Certain weeds hint at soil conditions — e.g. many sedges and rushes point to waterlogging; Striga thrives where soil fertility is low. Use them as clues, then confirm with a test.
In Kenya amaranth (terere) and African nightshade (managu) are valued leafy vegetables; in India many 'weeds' are eaten or used as fodder.
The store of live weed seeds and buds in the soil. Most weeds that appear each season come from this bank, so long-term success means stopping new seed being added.
Seeds shed in past seasons that lie dormant at different depths. Only a small share germinates each year; the rest can wait for years.

manas.q: What is the weed seed bank?

children.note: A few plants left to flower can refill the bank. The old saying is 'one year's seeding, seven years' weeding'.

manas.q: Why must weeds be removed before they set seed?

children.note: Turning soil brings buried seeds to the light and triggers a flush of germination. Shallow cultivation and less tillage expose fewer seeds.
Couch grass, nutsedge and similar weeds spread by rhizomes, tubers or runners. Chopping them with a rotavator can multiply them; exhaust them by repeated removal instead.
The window in the crop's life when weeds must be kept down to avoid yield loss. Weeds before or after it do much less harm.
Weeds that emerge with the crop and stay through the early weeks cut yield most; once the crop canopy closes, later weeds matter less.

manas.q: What is the critical period for weed control?

links.label: 📄 Source: Knezevic et al. 2002, Weed Science

children.note: Weed early and on time — usually the first weeks after emergence or transplanting; exact timing differs by crop, season and weed pressure.

links.label: 📄 Source: Knezevic et al. 2002, Weed Science

children.note: Transplanted vegetables and rice start ahead of the weeds, which makes early weeding easier than in direct-sown crops.
The cheapest weed is the one that never arrives. Stop seeds entering the field and give weeds no gap.
Buy certified or well-cleaned seed; weedy home-saved seed and seedlings spread weeds like Striga and dodder.

manas.q: Name two ways weed seeds arrive on a farm.

children.note: A compost heap that heats up well (around 55°C or more, turned) kills most weed seeds. Cold heaps and raw manure can spread them.
Wash ploughs, tractors and boots between fields, especially after working in Parthenium or Striga patches.
Prepare the bed, let rain or irrigation trigger a weed flush, kill it with a very shallow hoe or flame, then sow without stirring deeper soil.

manas.q: How does a stale seedbed work?

children.note: Cut or graze edges and bunds before weeds seed, while leaving some flowering strips for beneficial insects.
Covering the soil blocks light so weed seeds do not germinate, and also saves water and feeds soil life.
Straw, grass, crop residues, leaves or wood chips. A thick layer (several cm) is needed to suppress weeds; top it up as it rots.

manas.q: Why must an organic mulch be thick?

children.note: Hay or grass cut after seeding can sow new weeds. Use residues collected before flowering or composted material.
Generally allowed under organic standards if it is non-PVC (e.g. polyethylene) and fully removed after use. Never burn it or plough it in; check your standard for biodegradable films.

manas.q: What rules apply to plastic mulch in organic farming?

children.note: Black tarps laid on beds for some weeks kill emerging weeds (occultation). Clear plastic on moist soil in hot sun heats it enough to kill many seeds (solarisation).
Living plants that fill the gap so weeds cannot grow, while adding organic matter and often nitrogen.
They shade the soil, take up resources first, and some release chemicals from residues that slow weed germination.
Fast, dense crops such as buckwheat, cowpea, velvet bean (Mucuna) or sweet potato that close the canopy quickly and choke weeds.

manas.q: Give two examples of smother crops.

children.note: A thick cereal rye or rye-vetch cover is flattened with a roller-crimper and the cash crop planted through the mat — used on organic farms in temperate regions.
Mucuna, lablab, Desmodium and dolichos are used as cover and fodder legumes; they suppress weeds and fix nitrogen.
Growing two or more crops together closes the canopy sooner and leaves less space and light for weeds.
Maize with beans, cowpea or groundnut covers the ground better than maize alone, and the legume adds nitrogen.
A low legume grown between crop rows (e.g. Desmodium in maize) keeps weeds down all season.
Physical removal is the backbone of organic weed control. Tools work best on tiny weeds in dry, sunny weather.
Cheap and universal; a sharp, shallow cut is better than deep digging that brings up new seeds and damages crop roots.
Push-pull blades slice weeds just below the surface with little effort, ideal for vegetable beds.
A hoe blade on a wheel lets one person weed long rows standing up, much faster than a hand hoe.
Cono and rotary weeders are pushed between rice rows (as in SRI); they uproot weeds and churn them into the mud, also aerating the soil.

manas.q: What does a cono weeder do in rice?

children.note: Seedlings just germinated are killed by the lightest touch. A few minutes early saves hours later.

manas.q: When is the best time to hoe weeds?

children.note: Tine weeders, finger weeders and inter-row cultivators do the same job on larger farms.
Short bursts of heat burst weed cells; the plant wilts and dies within a day or two. Allowed in organic farming.
A gas burner passes quickly over the weeds — they are heated, not burnt to ash. Squeezing a leaf leaves a thumbprint if it worked.

manas.q: Does flame weeding need to burn weeds to ash?

children.note: Broadleaf seedlings at an early leaf stage; pre-emergence in slow crops like carrots and onions, just before the crop appears.
Grasses and perennials regrow from protected growing points. Keep fire risk in mind in dry residues and windy weather.
Steam and hot water are used on small areas and in greenhouses; solarisation uses the sun.
Animals can turn weeds into meat, milk or eggs.
Grazing in orchards, plantations and after harvest keeps weeds short; poultry also eat seeds and insects.
Keep stock off crops they damage, avoid toxic weeds (e.g. Lantana), and follow organic rules on manure near produce for fresh eating.
Some plants release chemicals from roots or residues that stop other plants germinating or growing.
Rye and sorghum residues and some brassicas can suppress small-seeded weeds for some weeks.

manas.q: What is allelopathy?

children.note: Desmodium root exudates cause Striga seeds to germinate and then block them from attaching to maize roots.

links.label: 📄 Source: Khan et al. 2014, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B

children.note: The same chemicals can slow small-seeded crops sown straight into the residues; leave a gap or transplant.
A parasitic weed that steals water and nutrients from cereal roots. In East Africa it is one of the biggest causes of maize and sorghum yield loss.
Striga hermonthica and S. asiatica attack maize, sorghum, millet, rice and sugarcane; S. gesnerioides attacks cowpea.

manas.q: Which crops does Striga hermonthica attack?

links.label: 📄 Source: Nzioki et al. 2016, Frontiers in Plant Science

children.note: Its tiny seeds germinate only when cereal roots release signals (strigolactones), then attach underground and drain the host before the weed even emerges.

links.label: 📄 Source: Cell 2025 — Striga resistance via lower strigolactone exudation

children.note: Stunted maize with wilting, yellowing or scorched-looking leaves, as if drought-stressed; later pink-purple flowered Striga plants appear around the stems.
Low soil fertility, continuous cereal cropping and huge, long-lived seed banks in the soil.
Maize intercropped with Desmodium and bordered by Napier or Brachiaria grass suppresses Striga, repels stemborers, adds nitrogen and produces fodder.

manas.q: Name the companion plants in push-pull.

links.label: 📄 Source: Khan et al. 2014, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B
📄 Source: Midega et al. 2018, Crop Protection

children.note: Resistant or tolerant maize and sorghum varieties support fewer Striga plants; combine them with push-pull and fertility building.

links.label: 📄 Source: Current progress in Striga management, Plant Physiology 2021

children.note: A Striga-specific fungus (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. strigae) can be coated onto seed, e.g. via inoculated toothpicks; on-farm trials showed less Striga emergence.

links.label: 📄 Source: Nzioki et al. 2016, Frontiers in Plant Science

children.note: Rotate with legumes (soybean, groundnut, cotton act as trap crops), add manure or compost, and hand-pull Striga before it flowers.
Herbicide-coated imazapyr-resistant maize controls Striga but uses a synthetic herbicide, so it is not allowed in certified organic farming.
Leafless root parasites (Orobanche and Phelipanche) that attack tomato, faba bean, sunflower, tobacco and mustard.
Pale or purplish flowering spikes appear at the crop base after damage is done; seeds stay alive in soil for many years.

manas.q: Why is broomrape hard to control?

links.label: 📄 Source: Fernández-Aparicio et al. 2016, Frontiers in Plant Science

children.note: Long rotations with non-hosts, clean seed, solarisation, catch crops that trigger germination, later sowing and hand removal before seed set.

links.label: 📄 Source: Fernández-Aparicio et al. 2016, Frontiers in Plant Science

children.note: Introduced plants that spread fast and harm crops, pastures, people and animals.
An annual from the Americas now spreading in Kenya, Ethiopia and India; it cuts crop and pasture yields and causes skin allergy and asthma.

manas.q: What health problems does Parthenium cause?

links.label: 📄 Source: Adkins & Shabbir 2014, Pest Management Science

children.note: Uproot before flowering, plant competitive pastures or cover crops, and use the leaf beetle Zygogramma where approved as biocontrol.

links.label: 📄 Source: Adkins & Shabbir 2014, Pest Management Science

children.note: A thorny ornamental shrub that forms thickets, poisons livestock and releases allelopathic chemicals. Cutting alone fails; uproot at the root crown and replant cover.

links.label: 📄 Source: Bhagwat et al. 2012, PLoS ONE
📄 Source: Allelopathy of Lantana camara, Plants 2021

children.note: Wear gloves, long sleeves and a mask for Parthenium; bag flowering plants; never move seeding plants or infested soil; only hot-compost them before seed set.

manas.q: How should Parthenium be handled safely?

children.note: What is and is not allowed.
Glyphosate, atrazine and all synthetic herbicides are prohibited in certified organic production.

manas.q: Are synthetic herbicides allowed in organic farming?

children.note: Well-run organic fields combine prevention, timing and tools to stay clean; weedy fields usually mean late or missed weeding.
No single tool wins; combine rotation, cover, timely tillage and seed-bank control.
Videos on organic and ecological weed management.
PlantVillage — how farmers set up push-pull to suppress Striga.
icipe — the drought-adapted push-pull system in East Africa.
Yielder/FiBL — practical organic weed control on Kenyan farms.
SARE — an organic grain farm in New York manages weeds with rotation and tools.
Purdue Extension — how and when to flame weed.
Digital Green — farmers in Bihar use the cono weeder.
Key sources.
Khan et al. 2014 — Desmodium and Napier grass against Striga and stemborers.
Knezevic et al. 2002 — the concept and how it is measured.
Adkins & Shabbir 2014 — biology, ecology and management.
Fernández-Aparicio et al. 2016 — mechanisms and strategies.

nodeData.note: Bees and other pollinators turn flowers into fruit and seed, and the same diverse habitat that feeds them also feeds the natural enemies of pests. Protecting them raises yields and quality, and beekeeping adds farm income.

children.note: Many fruit, vegetable, nut and seed crops need animals to move pollen; without them yields and fruit quality drop.
Of the leading global food crops, 87 depend on animal pollination to some degree, while staple cereals are wind- or self-pollinated.

manas.q: How many leading global food crops depend on animal pollination?

links.label: 📄 Source: Klein et al. 2007, Proc. R. Soc. B

children.note: Pollinator-dependent crops make up about 35% of global crop production volume — and much of the vitamins and variety in diets.

links.label: 📄 Source: Klein et al. 2007, Proc. R. Soc. B

children.note: Good pollination gives fuller, better-shaped fruit (e.g. even cucumbers and strawberries) and more seeds — poorly pollinated fruit is small or misshapen.

manas.q: What does poor pollination look like in fruit?

children.note: Pollinators support farmer and beekeeper incomes, food security and wider biodiversity.
Crops where bees make a big difference — important for Kenya's export and smallholder horticulture.
Flowers open female one day and male the next (A and B types like Hass and Fuerte). Bees moving pollen between types and trees raise fruit set.

manas.q: Why do avocado orchards need bees?

children.note: Yellow passion fruit is self-incompatible and relies on large carpenter bees; honeybees are less effective. Low fruit set often means too few carpenter bees.

manas.q: Which bees pollinate yellow passion fruit best?

children.note: Arabica can self-pollinate but bee visits improve fruit set and bean size; Robusta needs cross-pollination.
Pumpkin, melon, watermelon, cucumber and squash have separate male and female flowers; each female flower needs several bee visits.

manas.q: Why do cucurbits need bee visits?

children.note: Partly self-incompatible; cross-pollination by bees improves nut set, so mixed varieties and hives help.
Mango, apple, sunflower seed, canola, tomato (buzz pollination) and many legumes also benefit.
The most important pollinators in farming. Kenya has honeybees, stingless bees and hundreds of wild bee species.
Apis mellifera; in Kenya the native African subspecies (A. m. scutellata) is productive but defensive. Colonies live in hives of thousands of workers.

manas.q: Which honeybee subspecies is native to Kenya?

children.note: Small tropical bees (Meliponini) with no working sting; they nest in tree hollows, walls or the ground and pollinate many crops.
Keeping stingless bees in boxes. Honey yields are small but the honey sells at a premium; colonies are safe near homes and schools.

manas.q: What is meliponiculture?

children.note: Large Xylocopa bees nesting in dead wood; key pollinators of passion fruit and good buzz pollinators. Keep dead logs and stems for them.
Sweat bees, leafcutter, mason and mining bees nest alone in soil or stems. Wild bees boost fruit set even where honeybees are plentiful.
Not only bees carry pollen.
Hoverflies and other flies pollinate many crops; tiny midges are the main pollinators of cocoa.
Visit flowers by day and night; moths pollinate some night-flowering plants.
Beetles pollinate some tree crops; sunbirds visit many flowers; bats pollinate baobab and some tropical fruits.
Pollinators are declining in many regions from several pressures acting together.
Neonicotinoids are systemic — they reach pollen and nectar — and harm bees even at low doses. Not allowed in organic farming.

manas.q: Why are neonicotinoids especially risky for bees?

links.label: 📄 Source: Wood & Goulson 2017, Env. Sci. Pollut. Res.

children.note: Organic-allowed products can still harm bees: pyrethrins and spinosad are toxic on contact while wet, and neem can affect brood. Timing matters.

manas.q: Can organic insecticides harm bees?

links.label: 📄 Source: Christen et al. 2019, J. Hazardous Materials
📄 Source: Tschoeke et al. 2019, Environmental Pollution

children.note: Clearing hedges, bush and wild flowers removes food and nest sites; a single crop gives food for only a few weeks.

links.label: 📄 Source: Klein et al. 2007, Proc. R. Soc. B

children.note: Removing all flowering weeds and strips leaves pollinators without food between crop blooms.
Varroa mites and the viruses they carry weaken honeybee colonies; droughts and shifting seasons upset flowering.
Small changes in farm practice keep pollinators safe and abundant.
Spray only when needed, late evening when bees have stopped flying, never on open flowers, and when it is calm to avoid drift.

manas.q: When is the safest time to spray near bees?

children.note: Cut flowering weeds under orchard trees before spraying so bees are not foraging there.
Prefer Bt, entomopathogenic fungi, traps and natural enemies; read the bee warning on every label.
Tell neighbours with hives before spraying so they can close or move them.
Plant native flowers, hedges and flowering cover crops that bloom at different times. They support pollinators and pest enemies.

manas.q: How do flower strips help a farm?

links.label: 📄 Source: Albrecht et al. 2020, Ecology Letters

children.note: Leave patches of bare, undisturbed soil for ground bees, dead wood for carpenter bees, and hollow stems or bee hotels for solitary bees.
Provide a shallow water source with stones or sticks for landing, away from spray areas.
Bees add a product line without needing extra land, and they raise yields of nearby crops.
Traditional log hives, the Kenya top-bar hive (KTBH) and frame (Langstroth) hives; frame hives give cleaner honey and easier inspection.

manas.q: Name the three main hive types used in Kenya.

children.note: Honey, beeswax, propolis and pollen; stingless bee honey earns a premium price.
Place hives near forage and water, shaded, and away from homes, roads and tethered livestock because African honeybees can be defensive.
Organic standards require mainly organic or wild forage around the apiary (for example within 3 km under EU rules) and organic wax and treatments.
KALRO and county extension offer training; farmers' groups and cooperatives help with processing and marketing.
Renting or placing hives in crops at flowering — an extra income for beekeepers and a yield gain for growers.
Strong colonies are moved into the crop as flowering starts and removed afterwards; growers agree no-spray periods.
Honeybees supplement but do not replace wild pollinators — wild insect visits raised fruit set about twice as much.

manas.q: Can honeybees replace wild pollinators?

children.note: The same diverse farm that feeds pollinators also feeds natural enemies of pests.
A global synthesis found that the number of pollinator and natural-enemy species directly supports pollination, pest control and yield.

manas.q: Why does species richness matter for yields?

links.label: 📄 Source: Dainese et al. 2019, Science Advances

children.note: Up to half of the loss of pollination and pest-control services in simplified landscapes was linked to species loss.

links.label: 📄 Source: Dainese et al. 2019, Science Advances

children.note: Adult hoverflies, parasitic wasps and lacewings need nectar and pollen; flower strips near crops bring them in.

links.label: 📄 Source: Albrecht et al. 2020, Ecology Letters

children.note: Desmodium and Napier grass in maize repel and trap pests while attracting their natural enemies.

links.label: 📄 Source: Khan et al. 2014, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B

children.note: Common errors.
Natural does not mean harmless; follow label timing even for botanicals.
Diverse wild pollinators remain essential; protect their habitat too.
Burning or smoking out wild colonies destroys free pollinators; call a beekeeper to relocate them.
Videos on pollinators and beekeeping.
FAO — why protecting pollinators is vital for food.
CGTN Africa — how meliponiculture helps farmers and ecosystems.
GIZ Kenya — parts and use of the frame hive.
Project Integrated Crop Pollination — adding flowers on farms for bees.
Minnesota Dept. of Agriculture — practical spray precautions.
Plant & Food Research (NZ) — getting more fruit set in avocado.
Key sources.
Klein et al. 2007 — how much crops depend on pollinators.
Potts et al. 2016 — threats and responses, from the IPBES assessment.
Dainese et al. 2019 — richness of pollinators and enemies supports yields.
Garibaldi et al. 2013 — wild insects across 41 crop systems.

nodeData.note: Organic production guides: maize, beans & grain legumes, rice, sugarcane, potato.

children.note: How to grow maize organically: varieties, soil and nutrition, water, pests, diseases, Striga, safe drying and storage, and markets — with Kenya and India notes.
How to grow common beans and other grain legumes — cowpea, pigeon pea, green gram and chickpea — organically, using nodule bacteria, healthy soil and natural pest control.
How to grow rice organically: SRI, Azolla and blue-green algae for nitrogen, water-saving irrigation, and biological control of blast, borers and hoppers, with Kenya (Mwea) and India notes.
How to grow sugarcane organically: clean bud-chip seed, press mud and legumes, Gluconacetobacter, trash mulching instead of burning, and ratoon care, with Kenya and India notes.

How to grow Irish potato organically, from clean seed to storage: climate, soil, organic nutrition with biofertilizers, water, the main pests and diseases with organic control, and markets in Kenya, India and beyond.

nodeData.note: How to grow maize organically: varieties, soil and nutrition, water, pests, diseases, Striga, safe drying and storage, and markets — with Kenya and India notes.

children.note: Maize (Zea mays) is a grass and the main staple cereal of East and Southern Africa, also a major food, feed and starch crop in India and worldwide.
Maize uses the efficient C4 photosynthesis pathway and is wind-pollinated: pollen from the tassel falls on the silks of the cob.

manas.q: How is maize pollinated?

children.note: Hybrid seed gives higher yields but must be bought new each season; saved seed of open-pollinated varieties (OPVs) stays true to type and can be replanted.

manas.q: Why can a farmer replant OPV maize seed but not hybrid seed?

children.note: KALRO and seed companies release varieties by zone: late highland hybrids (e.g. H614D), mid-altitude hybrids (e.g. H513) and early dryland types (e.g. DH04, Katumani Composite B, an OPV).
Most Indian maize is single-cross hybrid; ICAR has released quality-protein maize (QPM) and specialty types such as sweet corn and baby corn.
Public breeding (CIMMYT and national programmes) has released drought- and heat-tolerant maize for tropical rain-fed farms.
Genetically modified (e.g. Bt) maize is prohibited under all organic standards, so organic farmers need verified non-GM, untreated seed.

manas.q: Can Bt maize be grown on a certified organic farm?

children.note: Maize grows best in warm, sunny seasons with steady rain and deep, fertile, well-drained soil.
Maize is a warm-season crop that is killed by frost and grows slowly in cold highlands; very hot, dry winds at flowering cause poor seed set.
Late highland types need a long wet season; early types fit short rains or dry zones where the season may end early.
Deep, well-drained loams rich in organic matter suit it best; maize hates waterlogging and suffers on compacted or very acid soils.

manas.q: Name two soil conditions maize does not tolerate.

children.note: A slightly acid to neutral soil suits maize; on strongly acid soils (common in western Kenya) liming and organic matter improve yields.
Maize is direct-sown; good seedbed, timing and spacing set the yield before any input is applied.
Reduced tillage with crop residues on the surface keeps moisture and soil life; deep ploughing every season burns organic matter.
Early planting gives the most yield and lets the crop escape later stemborer and fall armyworm peaks.

manas.q: Why does early planting help maize against pests?

children.note: A common Kenyan recommendation is rows 75 cm apart with one seed every 25 cm (or two every 50 cm), sown about 5 cm deep.
Placing well-made compost or manure in the planting hole or furrow puts nutrients where young roots are.
Beans, cowpea, pigeon pea or desmodium between maize rows add nitrogen, cover soil and reduce pests and Striga.

links.label: 📄 Source: Pest Manag. Sci. 2021 (Desmodium, beans and FAW)

children.note: Maize is a heavy feeder, especially of nitrogen; organic plans build soil fertility over seasons rather than feeding only the crop.
Grain carries away most of the N and P; the stover holds much of the K, so returning stover or composting it saves potassium.

manas.q: Which part of the maize plant holds much of the potassium?

children.note: Yellowing starts at the tip of older, lower leaves and runs down the midrib in a V shape.

manas.q: What does nitrogen deficiency look like on maize leaves?

children.note: Well-made compost or farmyard manure at planting is the base; uncomposted manure can carry weeds and burn seedlings.
Rotations with legumes, mucuna or lablab cover crops, and Tithonia leaves (used in Kenya) supply nitrogen for the next maize.
Rapid growth before tasselling needs most nitrogen: side-dress compost, liquid manure or plant tea around knee height.
Living inputs that help maize take up nitrogen and phosphorus.
Coat seed with Azospirillum or Azotobacter plus PSB in a sticker just before sowing, in the shade.

manas.q: Which biofertilizers are used as seed treatment for maize?

children.note: Mix biofertilizers or Trichoderma with compost and apply in the furrow at planting so they colonise the roots.
Arbuscular mycorrhiza helps maize take up phosphorus and water; reduced tillage keeps the fungal network alive.
Azospirillum lives on cereal roots, fixes some nitrogen and boosts root hairs; it complements, not replaces, manure.
A 2022 study found nitrogen-fixing bacteria living in maize stem sap; still research, not a field product yet.
Most maize is rain-fed; the key is to keep water in the soil and protect the flowering stage.
Drought at tasselling and silking causes the biggest yield losses because silks dry out and grains do not set.

manas.q: At which growth stage is maize most sensitive to drought?

children.note: Zai pits, tied ridges and mulch catch rain where it falls and help maize in dry areas.
Standing water for a few days damages roots and causes yellowing; drain low spots or plant on ridges.
Caterpillars dominate in the field, weevils and the larger grain borer in store.
Ragged holes and wet sawdust-like frass in the whorl; larva has an inverted Y on the head and four dots near the tail.
Early planting, scouting, crushing egg masses and young larvae, Bt or neem sprays into the whorl, and natural enemies.
Climate-adapted push–pull with Desmodium and Brachiaria reduced fall armyworm damage in East African trials.
Full guide to fall armyworm, stemborers and other caterpillars.
Window panes and shot holes in leaves, 'dead heart' in young plants, tunnels in stems and broken tassels.
Push–pull, destroying or composting old stalks, early planting and the parasitic wasp Cotesia.

manas.q: How do old maize stalks help stemborers survive?

children.note: Cutworms cut seedlings at soil level at night; termites attack roots and lodged plants in dry spells.
Guide to cutworms, termites, white grubs and other soil pests.
Corn leaf aphids colonise tassels; leafhoppers spread maize streak virus.
Aphids, leafhoppers and thrips and their natural enemies.
Store pests that bore into grain and turn it to powder; the larger grain borer can destroy unshelled cobs fast.
Hermetic storage, drying and other organic storage methods.
Viruses, leaf blights, rusts and ear rots are the main maize diseases worldwide.
Two viruses together (MCMV plus a potyvirus such as SCMV); leaves yellow from the margins, then whole plants dry up and cobs are empty.
MLN was reported in Bomet, Kenya in 2011 and spread to neighbouring countries.

manas.q: Which two viruses together cause maize lethal necrosis?

children.note: Certified clean seed, tolerant varieties, no continuous maize (rotate with legumes), a maize-free break and removing sick plants.
How viruses spread and how to manage vectors organically.
Narrow broken yellow streaks along the veins; spread by Cicadulina leafhoppers, worst in late-planted crops.

manas.q: Which insect spreads maize streak virus?

children.note: Grey leaf spot gives long rectangular grey lesions limited by veins; northern leaf blight gives long cigar-shaped tan lesions.
Resistant varieties, rotation, burying or composting infected residues and wider spacing for air flow.
Leaf blights, their look-alikes and organic control.
Rust gives brick-red powdery pustules on both leaf surfaces; downy mildew (important in India) gives pale streaks and white growth.
Recognising and managing mildews and rusts.
Pink, white, green or grey mould on cobs; Aspergillus flavus can make aflatoxin, a poison you cannot see.
Aflatoxin-contaminated maize caused deadly acute poisoning outbreaks in Kenya in 2004–2005.

manas.q: Why is mouldy maize dangerous even after cooking?

children.note: Spreading native non-toxic Aspergillus flavus strains in the field crowds out toxic ones; products are registered in several African countries.
Avoid drought stress, control insects that damage cobs, harvest on time and don't leave cobs in wet fields.
Weeds compete hardest in the first weeks; parasitic Striga is the most damaging weed of African maize.
Keep maize clean for roughly the first 4–6 weeks; later weeds cost less yield.

manas.q: When must maize be kept weed-free?

children.note: A purple-flowered parasite attached to maize roots; the maize stunts and wilts before Striga even emerges.
Root exudates of Desmodium intercrops trigger Striga seeds to germinate and stop them attaching, depleting the seed bank.

manas.q: How does Desmodium reduce Striga?

children.note: Pull Striga before it seeds, add manure, rotate with trap crops like cowpea or soybean, and use tolerant varieties.
Weed ecology and organic weed control.
Residue mulch and legume intercrops shade out weeds and protect soil between weedings.
Most aflatoxin and insect damage happens after harvest, so drying and storage decide grain quality.
Grain is mature when a black layer forms at the base of the kernel; then dry it in the field or on racks.

manas.q: What sign shows maize grain is physiologically mature?

children.note: Dry cobs on tarpaulins, raised racks or cribs; soil contact spreads Aspergillus and re-wets grain.
Shelled grain should be dry enough to rattle and crack between the teeth; moisture meters are more reliable.
Remove mouldy, insect-damaged and shrivelled cobs and grain; they carry most of the toxin.
Airtight bags or metal silos starve insects of oxygen and keep grain safe without chemicals.

manas.q: How do hermetic bags kill storage insects?

children.note: Organic maize is mostly sold locally or as feed; the premium depends on clean grain and good records.
East African and EU standards set strict maximum aflatoxin levels; mouldy grain can be rejected or destroyed.
Organic poultry and dairy farms need certified maize, making feed a key outlet.
Kenya exports baby corn and sweet corn to Europe as vegetables; residues and quality rules apply as for other fresh produce.
Use non-GM untreated seed, keep a buffer from GM or sprayed fields, record inputs and follow your standard.
Short videos from research and extension organisations.
How Desmodium and Brachiaria control Striga and stemborers in maize.
CIMMYT on MLN symptoms, spread and how farmers can prevent it.
University of Nebraska shows how to identify grey leaf spot lesions.
Doubling over mature stalks so cobs dry in the field and shed rain.
How to dry and store maize to avoid aflatoxin.
Simple steps for clean, dry, pest-free maize storage.
Reliable sources for deeper study.
Manuals and evidence on push–pull for stemborers, Striga and fall armyworm.
Review of the MLN outbreak, its viruses and management.
FAO guidance on monitoring and managing fall armyworm.
Free Kenyan site on organic and ecological crop production and pest control.
Background on maize biology, history and uses.

nodeData.note: How to grow common beans and other grain legumes — cowpea, pigeon pea, green gram and chickpea — organically, using nodule bacteria, healthy soil and natural pest control.

children.note: Grain legumes (pulses) feed people with protein and feed the soil with nitrogen fixed by root-nodule bacteria.
Phaseolus vulgaris, grown as dry beans and as green French beans; the most eaten grain legume in East Africa.
Bush types mature fast; climbing beans need stakes but can yield much more on small plots, popular in Rwanda and western Kenya.

manas.q: Why do farmers on small plots grow climbing beans?

children.note: KALRO releases include Rosecoco and Mwitemania types for the highlands, KAT B1 and KAT B9 for dry areas, and iron-rich Nyota.
Vigna unguiculata: the most drought- and heat-tolerant pulse; leaves are eaten as a vegetable and grain is dried.

manas.q: Which grain legume tolerates the most heat and drought?

links.label: 📄 Source: Front. Plant Sci. 2016 (cowpea in Africa)

children.note: Cajanus cajan: a deep-rooted shrubby legume grown in dry eastern Kenya and across India (tur/arhar), often intercropped with maize or sorghum.
Vigna radiata (mung bean, ndengu): a fast, short-season pulse for dry lowlands; Kenya grows it widely in Eastern region.
Cicer arietinum: India's biggest pulse, grown in the cool dry season on stored soil moisture; also grown on black cotton soils in Kenya.

manas.q: When is chickpea grown in India?

children.note: Each pulse has its own niche; all hate waterlogging and acid, poor soils limit nodulation.
It grows best in mild mid-altitude climates; heat and drought at flowering cause flower and pod drop.
Cowpea, green gram and pigeon pea suit hot, drier lowlands; chickpea suits cool, dry seasons.
Well-drained loams with good organic matter; waterlogged soils rot roots and kill nodules.

manas.q: Why are legumes poor on waterlogged soils?

children.note: Very acid soils hurt both the plant and its rhizobia; liming and manure help beans on acid Kenyan highland soils.

links.label: 📄 Source: Microbiol. Mol. Biol. Rev. 1999 (rhizobia under stress)

children.note: Clean seed, good spacing and the right partner crops give a healthy stand.
Many bean diseases (anthracnose, blights, BCMV) are seed-borne: use certified or carefully selected seed from healthy plants.

manas.q: Why does clean seed matter so much for beans?

children.note: Bush beans are commonly sown about 45–50 cm between rows and 10–15 cm within the row; pigeon pea needs much wider spacing.
Beans or cowpea between maize rows give two crops, fix nitrogen and can reduce fall armyworm on the maize.

links.label: 📄 Source: Pest Manag. Sci. 2021 (Desmodium, beans and FAW)

children.note: Do not plant beans after beans; rotating with cereals breaks root rot and disease cycles.
Legumes make most of their own nitrogen if well nodulated, but they still need phosphorus, potassium and micronutrients.

children.topic: Common bean is a weak fixer
children.note: Common bean fixes less nitrogen than cowpea, soybean or pigeon pea, so it responds to compost and good nodulation.
Nodules need lots of P and energy; P shortage is the most common limit to N fixation on African soils.

manas.q: Which nutrient most often limits nitrogen fixation in legumes?

links.label: 📄 Source: Microbiol. Mol. Biol. Rev. 1999 (rhizobia under stress)

children.note: Molybdenum is part of the nitrogenase enzyme; Ca and S also support nodules. Acid soils often lack Mo.
Apply well-made compost in the furrow at planting; too much fresh nitrogen reduces nodulation.
In one study biochar raised the share of nitrogen beans fixed from the air.

links.label: 📄 Source: Biol. Fertil. Soils 2007 (biochar and bean BNF)

children.note: Living inputs for pulses, applied mostly on the seed.
Coat seed with the right Rhizobium in a sugar or gum sticker, in the shade, and sow the same day.

manas.q: How long can inoculated seed wait before sowing?

children.topic: Match the strain to the crop
children.note: Each pulse needs its own group: Rhizobium for common bean, Bradyrhizobium for cowpea, green gram and pigeon pea, Mesorhizobium for chickpea.

manas.q: Which rhizobium group nodulates chickpea?

children.note: Cowpea often nodulates with native soil bacteria, so it responds less to inoculation than common bean or soybean.
PSB with rhizobium improves P supply; Trichoderma seed treatment protects against root rots — apply it first, then rhizobium.
Dig up a plant: active nodules are pink to red inside; white, green or no nodules mean poor fixation.

manas.q: What colour are active nodules inside?

children.note: Pulses use less water than cereals but suffer at flowering and pod fill.
Flowering and pod filling are the most sensitive stages; stress then drops flowers and leaves pods empty.

manas.q: When are beans most sensitive to drought?

children.note: Mulch and tied ridges keep moisture; avoid overhead watering late in the day, which favours leaf diseases.
Plant on raised beds in wet areas; even short waterlogging invites root rots.
Bean fly and aphids attack early; pod borers attack flowers and pods; bruchids attack in store.
Ophiomyia flies lay eggs in leaves; maggots tunnel to the stem base, which swells and cracks, and seedlings wilt and die.
Plant early, earth up soil around stems to promote new roots, mulch, keep plants vigorous with compost, and grow tolerant varieties.

manas.q: How does earthing up help beans against bean fly?

children.note: Soil and stem-base pests and how to manage them.
Black aphids on shoots and pods spread bean common mosaic virus; thrips scar flowers and cause flower drop.
Aphids, thrips, whiteflies and their natural enemies.
Larvae web flowers, pods and leaves together and bore into pods; a major pest of cowpea and pigeon pea.
Parasitic wasps (e.g. Apanteles taragamae introduced in Benin), neem and Bt sprays at flowering.

links.label: 📄 Source: J. Chem. Ecol. 2010 (Apanteles vs Maruca)

children.note: Green to brown larvae make round holes in pods of chickpea and pigeon pea and eat the seeds.
Pheromone traps, bird perches, hand shaking of pigeon pea plants onto sheets, HearNPV and neem sprays.

manas.q: Name a specific virus product for Helicoverpa.

children.note: Caterpillar biology and organic control in detail.
Ootheca and other beetles chew round holes in leaves of young beans and cowpea.
Beetle pests and organic control.
Small beetles lay eggs on seeds; larvae eat inside and adults leave round exit holes.
Hermetic storage and other organic store protection.
Many bean diseases ride on seed and splash with rain, so clean seed and dry foliage are the first defence.
Angular leaf spot: brown angular spots boxed in by veins. Anthracnose: dark sunken pod lesions and blackened veins under leaves.
Clean seed, resistant varieties, rotation, removing debris and staying out of the field when leaves are wet.

manas.q: Why stay out of a bean field when leaves are wet?

children.note: Fungal leaf and pod blights in detail.
Common blight: brown leaf patches with yellow edges. Halo blight: small spots with a wide yellow halo; both seed-borne.
Bacterial diseases and organic options, including copper limits.
Rust gives rusty-brown powdery pustules under leaves; powdery mildew (common in green gram) gives white dusty patches.
Recognition and organic control of mildews and rusts.
Fusarium, Pythium and Rhizoctonia rot the roots: plants yellow, stunt and die in patches, worst on tired, wet soils.
Rotation, raised beds, compost, Trichoderma seed treatment and tolerant climbing varieties.
Root rot pathogens and soil-health solutions.
Chickpea and pigeon pea wilt: plants droop and dry while the inner stem shows brown streaks.
Wilt diseases and how to tell them apart.
BCMV (bean mosaic, aphid- and seed-borne), yellow mosaic of green gram (whiteflies, India) and pigeon pea sterility mosaic (mites).

manas.q: Which vector spreads yellow mosaic of green gram?

children.note: Viruses, their vectors and prevention.
Pulses are short and grow slowly at first, so early weed control is vital.
Two weedings in the first four to six weeks usually protect most of the yield.
Working among wet bean plants spreads bacterial blights and anthracnose.
Striga gesnerioides and Alectra attack cowpea roots in dry Africa; use resistant varieties and rotation.

manas.q: Which parasitic weeds attack cowpea?

children.note: Timely harvest and dry storage protect grain from shattering, mould and bruchids.
Harvest when most pods are dry and yellow-brown; pigeon pea and cowpea are often picked in several rounds.
Dry plants on tarpaulins, thresh by beating gently in bags, then dry grain until it is hard.
Airtight triple-layer bags or sealed drums kill bruchids by cutting off oxygen, without chemicals.

manas.q: Why do airtight bags stop bruchids?

children.note: Coating seed with vegetable oil, mixing with ash, or using aromatic plants like basil can deter bruchids.

links.label: 📄 Source: J. Stored Prod. Res. 2001 (basil oils vs bruchids)

children.note: Heating grain in the sun under clear plastic kills bruchid eggs and larvae inside cowpea seeds.
Pulses sell well locally; French beans are a major Kenyan export with strict rules.
Kenya exports fresh green beans to Europe; buyers demand GLOBALG.A.P., traceability and KEPHIS inspection.
EU limits are very low; consignments with residues are rejected, so organic and biological control is a market advantage.

manas.q: Why do EU MRLs favour biological pest control?

children.note: India is the largest pulse producer and consumer, so tur, moong and chana have strong local demand.
Organic needs untreated seed and approved inoculants; chemical seed dressings are not allowed.
Short videos from research and extension organisations.
How to stake climbing beans for higher yields on small plots.
Natural ways to control aphids in beans and vegetables.
Step-by-step seed inoculation with rhizobium before sowing.
Animation on natural enemies and biopesticides for Maruca in cowpea.
Farmer video on controlling Helicoverpa pod borer in pigeon pea.
How to use airtight bags to keep bruchids out of stored pulses.
Reliable sources for deeper study.
Project resources on inoculating and growing legumes in Africa.
Free Kenyan site on organic pulse production and pest control.
Review of cowpea's role, constraints and breeding in sub-Saharan Africa.
Background on the common bean's biology and types.
Background on pigeon pea biology and uses.

nodeData.note: How to grow rice organically: SRI, Azolla and blue-green algae for nitrogen, water-saving irrigation, and biological control of blast, borers and hoppers, with Kenya (Mwea) and India notes.

children.note: Rice (Oryza sativa, plus African rice O. glaberrima) is a grass grown mostly in flooded paddies, but also in rainfed lowlands and uplands. It feeds more than half of the world.
Asian rice (Oryza sativa, with indica and japonica groups) dominates worldwide; African rice (O. glaberrima) was domesticated in West Africa and is hardier but lower yielding.

manas.q: Which two rice species are cultivated?

children.note: Irrigated lowland (most production), rainfed lowland, upland (dry fields, no flooding) and deep-water rice. Organic methods differ mainly in how water and weeds are handled.
Kenyan consumers pay a premium for aromatic Basmati, locally called Pishori, grown mainly under irrigation at Mwea. Non-aromatic types such as IR-lines are grown for yield.

manas.q: What do Kenyans call locally grown aromatic Basmati rice?

children.note: KALRO and partners have released higher-yielding, blast-tolerant lines (e.g. Komboka). Ask the scheme office or KALRO Mwea for seed suited to your block.
Widely grown examples include Swarna and Samba Mahsuri (non-aromatic) and Pusa Basmati types for export. State universities list varieties for each season and zone.
Prefer varieties with good blast and bacterial blight tolerance, strong roots and good tillering. Very high-input hybrids often disappoint without synthetic N.

manas.q: Which disease tolerances matter most when choosing an organic rice variety?

children.note: Rice is a warm-season crop that needs plenty of water. It tolerates flooding because its roots and stems carry air down through hollow tissue (aerenchyma).
Grows best in warm weather; cold nights at flowering cause empty grains, and very hot spells at flowering also reduce seed set.
Air channels (aerenchyma) carry oxygen from leaves to roots, so rice survives waterlogged soil that kills most crops.

manas.q: How do rice roots get oxygen in flooded soil?

children.note: Clay and clay-loam soils that hold water are ideal for paddies. Flooding brings soil pH towards neutral and makes P and iron more available.

Kenya's main rice area: the Mwea irrigation scheme in Kirinyaga County, started in 1954, fed by the Thiba river from Mount Kenya on heavy clay plains. Ahero and West Kano near Kisumu are other schemes.

manas.q: When was the Mwea irrigation scheme founded and which river feeds it?

links.label: 📄 Source: Wikipedia – Rice farming in Kenya

children.note: Good levelling and a healthy nursery are the foundation of organic rice; weak seedlings cannot outgrow weeds and pests.
A level field lets a shallow water layer cover all the soil evenly, so weeds are suppressed and water use falls.

manas.q: Why does field levelling matter so much in rice?

children.note: Ploughing in standing water makes a soft mud that holds water and buries weeds. Repeated puddling can damage soil structure for the next dry-season crop.
Float seed in salt water (a fresh egg should float); discard the light seeds that float and rinse the heavy ones. Heavy seed gives stronger seedlings.

manas.q: How do you separate heavy rice seed for sowing?

children.note: Treat soaked seed with Pseudomonas fluorescens or Trichoderma and Azospirillum/PSB before sowing in the nursery. Do not mix with chemical fungicides.
A well-drained nursery bed rich in compost gives sturdy seedlings. In SRI a small, mat-type nursery near the field is used.
Plant seedlings shallowly at even spacing in rows so a weeder can pass. Older seedlings recover more slowly from transplanting.
Seed can be broadcast or drilled into wet or dry soil, saving labour, but weeds become the main challenge in organic systems.
A set of practices developed in Madagascar by Fr. Henri de Laulanié: young single seedlings, wide spacing, moist not flooded soil, active weeding and organic matter.
Developed in Madagascar in the 1980s by the Jesuit priest Henri de Laulanié and later spread worldwide with support from Cornell University.

manas.q: Who developed SRI and where?

links.label: 📄 Source: Wikipedia – System of Rice Intensification

children.note: Transplant very young seedlings (around two leaves, often 8–12 days old), one per hill, gently and quickly so roots are not damaged.

manas.q: How old and how many seedlings per hill in SRI?

links.label: 📄 Source: Wikipedia – System of Rice Intensification

children.note: Wide spacing (often 25 × 25 cm or more) gives each plant room for roots and tillers and lets a weeder pass both ways.
Keep soil moist with intermittent irrigation instead of standing water during the vegetative stage, so roots get air and grow deeper.
A rotary or cono weeder is pushed between rows every 10–12 days; it kills weeds and aerates the soil. Weeds are returned as green manure.
Compost, manure and green manures feed the soil life that SRI depends on.
Aerated SRI soils favour beneficial root microbes; a review links much of the SRI benefit to the root microbiome.
Very high early yield claims were challenged by scientists; gains vary by site and skill. Water and seed savings are more consistent than yield records.
Feed the soil before planting, add biological N from Azolla, algae and bacteria during the crop, and recycle straw.
Most nitrogen and phosphorus leave in the grain, while most potassium and silicon stay in the straw. Returning straw recycles much of the K.

manas.q: Which nutrients stay mostly in rice straw?

children.note: Apply well-made compost or farmyard manure before final puddling so it is mixed into the mud.
Grow dhaincha (Sesbania) or sunn hemp for 6–8 weeks and plough it in before transplanting; it adds N and organic matter.

manas.q: Name two green manures ploughed in before rice.

children.note: Azolla is a floating fern that hosts the N-fixing cyanobacterium Anabaena. Grown in the paddy water alongside rice, it fixes nitrogen and is later trampled into the soil.

manas.q: Which cyanobacterium lives inside Azolla?

children.note: Besides N, an Azolla cover shades the water, suppresses weeds and keeps water pH from rising, which reduces ammonia loss.

links.label: 📄 Source: Biol Fertil Soils 1999 (BGA & Azolla review)

children.note: Blue-green algae (cyanobacteria such as Nostoc, Anabaena) are spread as soil-based flakes into the standing water after transplanting; they fix N in the flood water.

manas.q: What is algalization in rice?

children.note: Dip seedling roots in a slurry of Azospirillum and phosphate-solubilizing bacteria before transplanting.
Zinc deficiency (bronze, stunted seedlings; "khaira" in India) is common in flooded alkaline soils. Organic standards allow zinc salts only when deficiency is shown.
Rice takes up a lot of silicon, which stiffens leaves against blast and insects. Straw, husk ash and compost return silicon and K.
Rice uses more water than other crops, but continuous deep flooding is not needed for good yields.
Water shortage hurts most at panicle initiation and flowering. Drain about 1–2 weeks before harvest.
Let the field water drop below the surface, then re-flood. A perforated pipe (field water tube) shows the water level in the soil.

manas.q: What tool shows when to re-irrigate in AWD?

children.note: A meta-analysis found no significant yield loss when water was allowed to drop only to about 15 cm below the surface, with about 23% less water; severe drying cut yields by about 23%.

manas.q: How far can water drop in "safe" AWD?

children.note: AWD roughly halved methane emissions in a global meta-analysis, though nitrous oxide rose somewhat.

links.label: 📄 Source: Global Change Biology 2024 (AWD emissions meta-analysis)

children.note: Without standing water, weeds grow faster, so AWD and SRI need timely mechanical weeding.
Healthy, unsprayed paddies hold many spiders, dragonflies and parasitoids that keep most pests below damaging levels.
Yellow stem borer (Asia) and African stem borers (e.g. Maliarpha, Chilo) tunnel in stems.
Young plants show "deadhearts" (central shoot dries and pulls out); at heading, "whiteheads" are empty white panicles that stand upright.

manas.q: What are deadhearts and whiteheads in rice?

children.note: Collect egg masses from seedbeds, clip seedling leaf tips before transplanting, release Trichogramma egg parasitoid cards, cut stubble low after harvest.
Borers, armyworms and their organic control in detail.
Cnaphalocrocis caterpillars fold leaves lengthwise and scrape the green tissue, leaving white streaks. Usually controlled by natural enemies; avoid early sprays.
Nilaparvata lugens sucks sap at the plant base; patches dry out suddenly ("hopperburn"). Outbreaks follow excess N and insecticide sprays that kill spiders.

manas.q: Which two practices trigger brown planthopper outbreaks?

children.note: Balanced organic N, alleyways every few metres for air, draining the field for a few days, and conserving spiders and mirid predators.
Hoppers, bugs and aphids in detail.
Larvae turn the growing shoot into a hollow tube, the "onion leaf" or silver shoot. Use tolerant varieties and avoid staggered planting.
Rice bugs suck milky grains, leaving empty or spotted grain. Birds such as quelea in Africa raid ripening fields; synchronous planting and scaring help.
Most rice diseases are managed by resistant varieties, clean seed, balanced nutrition and good spacing.
Caused by the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae (Pyricularia). The most important rice disease worldwide.
Spindle- or eye-shaped leaf spots with grey centres and brown edges; "neck blast" rots the panicle neck so grains stay empty.

manas.q: Describe a rice blast leaf lesion.

children.note: High N, long leaf wetness, cool nights with dew, and dry-nursery or upland conditions.
Resistant varieties, moderate N, silicon from straw and husk ash, seed treatment and sprays with Pseudomonas fluorescens or Bacillus.
Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae: yellow stripes with wavy edges from the leaf tip down; young plants may wilt ("kresek"). Spreads with water and wind-driven rain.

manas.q: What does bacterial leaf blight look like on rice?

children.note: Rhizoctonia solani makes oval grey-green lesions with brown borders on the sheath near the water line, like snake skin. Wider spacing and less N help.
Bipolaris oryzae: small round brown spots. It is a sign of poor, nutrient-starved soils, especially low K and silicon.
An African virus first reported in Kenya in 1966: yellow-mottled leaves and stunting. Spread by beetles and by contact; use tolerant varieties and remove ratoons.

manas.q: Where was rice yellow mottle virus first reported?

children.note: Synthetic fungicides such as tricyclazole are not allowed in organic rice. Copper is allowed only within certifier limits.
General disease biology and organic control.
How bacterial diseases spread and are managed.
Weeds are the biggest yield limit in organic rice, especially without standing water.
A shallow, continuous water layer after transplanting stops most grass weeds from germinating.
Pushed between rows 2–4 times in the first 40 days; they bury weeds and aerate soil.

manas.q: When are rotary weeders used in rice?

children.note: Flood and prepare the land, let weeds sprout, then kill them with the final puddling before planting.
Rice-duck (aigamo) and rice-fish systems in Asia use animals to eat weeds and insects while adding manure.
Red or weedy rice looks like crop rice but shatters early. Use clean certified seed and transplant rather than broadcast.
Principles and tools for weed control.
Good timing and fast drying protect yield and quality, especially for premium aromatic rice.
Harvest when most grains (about 80–85%) are straw-coloured and hard. Late harvest causes shattering and cracked grains.
Dry paddy quickly to about 14% moisture for safe storage; slow or uneven drying causes mould and broken rice in milling.

manas.q: To what moisture content should paddy be dried for storage?

children.note: Airtight bags or silos starve insects of oxygen, an organic-allowed method against weevils and moths.
Rice weevil, grain moth and organic storage methods.
Return straw as mulch or compost instead of burning; burning wastes K and silicon and pollutes the air.
Organic rice earns more where buyers trust the label, mainly aromatic types.
