nodeData.note: Mango is a long-lived tropical fruit tree grown from Kenya's coast and Eastern region to all of India. Organic success rests on grafted trees, a low open canopy, timed water, weaver ants and area-wide fruit fly control.

children.note: Mango is a long-lived evergreen tree grown across the tropics and subtropics. Choosing the right variety and grafted planting material decides yield, market and pest pressure for decades.
Mango belongs to the Anacardiaceae, the same family as cashew. It originated in South and Southeast Asia, and India is still the largest producer.

manas.q: To which plant family does mango belong?

children.note: Indian-type mangoes usually have one embryo per seed, so seedlings differ from the parent. Many Southeast Asian types are polyembryonic and give true-to-type seedlings, which makes them useful as uniform rootstocks.

manas.q: Why are polyembryonic mango seeds useful for rootstocks?

children.note: Grafted varieties such as Apple, Ngowe, Kent, Tommy Atkins, Van Dyke and Keitt are widely grown in Kenya. Apple and Ngowe are local favourites; Kent and Tommy Atkins travel well for export and processing.
Alphonso, Kesar, Dasheri, Langra, Banganapalli and Totapuri dominate Indian orchards. TNAU also lists the dwarf hybrids Mallika and Amrapali, suited to closer planting.
Grafted trees start bearing in a few years and keep the variety true. Seedling trees take much longer, vary in quality and grow very tall, which makes spraying, pruning and harvest hard.

manas.q: Why should mango orchards be planted with grafted trees?

children.note: Mango loves heat and a dry spell before flowering. It tolerates poor soils but not waterlogging or frost.
A dry or cool period stops shoot growth and lets flower buds form. Areas with rain during flowering get poor fruit set and heavy anthracnose and powdery mildew.

manas.q: Which weather before flowering helps mango flower well?

children.note: Mango roots go deep, so deep soils with good drainage give long-lived trees. TNAU recommends red loamy soils with a pH of about 6.5–8.0.
Young trees are killed by frost, and strong wind at flowering and fruit set knocks off flowers and fruitlets. Windbreaks help on exposed sites.
A mango orchard is a 30-plus-year investment, so layout, planting material and pits deserve care.
Buy from a registered nursery (KEPHIS-inspected in Kenya) and check the graft union is healthy. Reject plants with black leaf spots, scale insects or malformed shoots.
Cleft or side-veneer grafting of scions onto vigorous local rootstock seedlings is standard. Use scions from healthy, high-yielding mother trees.
TNAU gives 7–10 m between trees for conventional planting and 5 × 5 m (400 trees/ha) for high-density orchards that are kept small by pruning.

manas.q: What spacing does TNAU give for high-density mango?

children.note: Dig large pits weeks before planting and refill with topsoil mixed with well-rotted compost or manure. This is the best moment to add mycorrhiza and other biofertilizers.
Before the canopy closes, legumes, vegetables or pineapple can earn income between rows. Keep them out of the tree basin and avoid tall crops that shade young trees.
Feed the soil with organic matter every year and correct micronutrients. Too much nitrogen gives leafy flushes instead of flowers.

TNAU gives 10 kg farmyard manure per tree in year 1, rising by 10 kg a year to 50 kg from year 6. Organic growers supply the nutrients through compost, manure and legumes instead of the NPK in that schedule.

manas.q: How much FYM per tree does TNAU suggest for a 6-year-old mango tree?

children.note: Main feeding goes on after harvest and pruning to support the new flush that will carry next year's flowers. Avoid heavy nitrogen just before flowering.
A thick mulch of grass, prunings or crop residues keeps the root zone moist and feeds soil life. Keep mulch a hand-width away from the trunk.
Sow legumes such as cowpea, lablab or sunn hemp between rows in the rains and slash them onto the basins. They add nitrogen and organic matter.
Mango often lacks boron (poor fruit set, cracked or deformed fruit) and zinc (small, narrow leaves). Confirm with a leaf test; organic standards allow trace-element salts when a need is shown.
Use microbes as helpers on top of compost, not as a replacement.
Mix mycorrhiza inoculum and a phosphate-solubilising bacteria product into the compost in the planting pit, so they colonise new roots.
Blend Azospirillum, PSB and potassium-mobilising bacteria with compost and spread in the moist basin after harvest. Keep them away from copper sprays.
How mycorrhizal fungi extend tree roots and how to inoculate.
How PSB release locked phosphorus and how to apply them.
Water decides fruit size, but a dry spell is needed for flowering. Timing matters more than quantity.
TNAU advises stopping irrigation for about 30 days before flowering to induce stress, then restarting once flowers appear.

manas.q: When should irrigation be held back in mango?

children.note: Regular water from fruit set to maturity cuts fruit drop and builds size. Drip with mulch is the most efficient.
Easing irrigation in the last weeks before harvest improves sweetness and keeping quality.
Mango flowers on mature shoot tips. Uniform, well-timed flowering gives a crop that can be protected and harvested together.
Shoots need to rest and harden for some months before they can flower. Late flushes after harvest often do not flower that season.
Many varieties give a heavy crop one year and little the next. Moderate crops, timely pruning and good feeding reduce the swing.

manas.q: What is alternate bearing in mango?

children.note: Flies, bees and other insects pollinate mango flowers. Keep flowering weeds and hedges nearby and do not spray at bloom.

Paclobutrazol (a synthetic growth regulator) and potassium nitrate sprays are used conventionally to force flowering. They are not allowed under organic standards; organic growers rely on stress, pruning and timing.

manas.q: Is paclobutrazol allowed in organic mango?

children.note: Protecting bees and flies that set fruit.
A low, open canopy lets light in, cuts disease and makes spraying and harvest easy.
Pinch the young tree at about knee-to-waist height and keep three or four well-spaced main branches. This builds a low, open frame.
Cut back shoots soon after harvest so new flushes have time to mature before the next flowering season.

manas.q: When is the best time to prune mango?

children.note: Remove crossing, dead and inward branches. Sun and air in the canopy dry leaves faster and reduce anthracnose and mildew.
Very tall, old trees can be cut back hard in stages and new shoots trained. They return to bearing in about two to three years.
Fruit flies, seed weevil, scales and hoppers are the main mango pests. Natural enemies, above all weaver ants, do much of the work in organic orchards.
Oriental fruit fly and mango fruit fly (Ceratitis cosyra) lay eggs in ripening fruit; maggots rot the pulp.
Small sting marks with sap, soft patches that spread under the skin, early fruit drop and maggots inside cut fruit.

manas.q: How do you recognise fruit fly damage on mango?

children.note: Collect fallen fruit every few days, use protein bait sprays and male lures, bag fruit, harvest at mature-green and keep weaver ants. Work with neighbours across the area.
Lures, baits, augmentoria and the icipe IPM package.
Sternochetus mangiferae is a weevil whose larva lives inside the seed. It is a quarantine pest for several export markets.
The fruit usually looks normal outside; the seed is eaten and holds the larva or adult. Infested fruits may drop early.

manas.q: Where does the mango seed weevil larva feed?

children.note: Adults hide under loose bark and in cracks between seasons and lay eggs on young fruit. Collect and destroy fallen fruit and seeds, and remove loose bark.

manas.q: How do organic farmers break the seed weevil cycle?

children.note: Other weevils and beetles and their organic control.
Oecophylla ants build leaf nests in the canopy and hunt fruit flies, seed weevils and bugs. A meta-analysis found ants generally reduce pests and plant damage.
Move nests from other trees, link trees with ropes or branches, and protect colonies from broad-spectrum sprays. Control competing ground ants.

manas.q: How can farmers spread weaver ants through a mango orchard?

children.note: Ants leave small dark marks on the skin. A study found these marks did not harm internal quality or storage life of the fruit.
Trials in Benin found fewer fruit fly-damaged mangoes where weaver ants were abundant, and a 2026 Thai study found chemical sprays did not outperform ant biocontrol.
White mango scale is a major pest in Kenya; hoppers and giant mealybug are serious in India. All suck sap and leave honeydew and sooty mould.
Prune infested shoots, band trunks against mealybug crawlers, conserve ladybirds and parasitic wasps, and use horticultural oil or neem when numbers build up.
Scales, mealybugs, hoppers and thrips in detail.
Anthracnose and powdery mildew cause the biggest losses, both linked to wet or humid weather at flowering.
Fungi of the Colletotrichum gloeosporioides group attack leaves, flowers and fruit. It is the most damaging mango disease worldwide.
Black spots on young leaves, blackened flower panicles and dark sunken patches on ripening fruit, often in tear-stain streaks.

manas.q: What does anthracnose look like on ripening mango?

children.note: The fungus enters young fruit in the field and stays dormant, only showing as the fruit ripens. So field control decides post-harvest losses.

manas.q: Why does mango anthracnose often appear only after harvest?

children.note: Prune for airflow, remove dead twigs and old fruit, and protect flowers and young fruit with copper (allowed with limits) or Bacillus biofungicides.
Hot-water treatment of fruit lowers anthracnose in storage. Research on chitosan coatings with plant essential oils is promising.
Anthracnose and other leaf and fruit spots.
A fungus (Erysiphe quercicola, long called Oidium mangiferae) that coats flowers and young fruit with white powder.
White powdery growth on flower stalks, young leaves and fruitlets, followed by browning and heavy flower and fruit drop.

manas.q: Which mango organs does powdery mildew damage most?

children.note: Start at early panicle stage with wettable sulphur or potassium bicarbonate. Bacillus subtilis and other biocontrol agents have shown control in field trials.
How mildews spread and how to manage them organically.
Xanthomonas causes raised black, cracked spots on leaves and fruit, spread by wind-driven rain. Windbreaks, clean planting material and copper help.
Bunchy, deformed flower panicles caused by Fusarium fungi, common in parts of India. Cut out and burn malformed panicles well below the affected part.
Weeds compete most with young trees. Mature trees mainly need a clean basin and short ground cover.
Keep the basin to the drip line weed-free with mulch rather than deep hoeing, which cuts feeder roots.
Slash or graze grass between rows and leave the cuttings as cover. Herbicides are not allowed in organic orchards.
Mulch, cover crops and mechanical weeding.
Most mango losses happen between the tree and the buyer. Careful picking and cool handling protect the price.
Shoulders rise above the stalk, the skin colour softens and the flesh near the seed turns yellow. Mature fruit is denser and sinks in water.

manas.q: Name two signs that a mango is mature for picking.

children.note: Pick by hand or with a padded picking pole, leaving a short stalk. This stops sap from running onto the skin.
The milky sap burns the skin and leaves dark marks. De-sap fruit stalk-down on racks, away from the soil.

manas.q: Why is mango placed stalk-down after picking?

children.note: Keep fruit in the shade in clean crates, never on bare ground. Grade, then cool as soon as possible to slow ripening.
Drying, pulp and juice turn surplus or off-grade fruit into income, as Makueni farmers in Kenya have shown.
Mango sells fresh at home, in regional and Middle East markets, and in Europe for high-quality, residue-free fruit.
Fruit flies and seed weevil decide market access. Interceptions in Europe have in the past led Kenya to suspend mango exports, so area-wide control matters.

manas.q: Which two mango pests most limit exports?

children.note: Exporters must register with the Horticultural Crops Directorate and pass KEPHIS phytosanitary inspection. Buyers often also need GlobalG.A.P.
APEDA runs export registration. Markets such as the USA and Japan require approved treatments like irradiation or vapour-heat for fruit flies.
Importing countries set maximum residue limits for each pesticide. Organic fruit avoids synthetic residues but copper and sulphur rules still apply.
Certification needs a conversion period and records of every input. Groups of smallholders can certify together under an internal control system.
How certification works in Kenya, India and for export.
Practical videos on mango growing, pests and harvest.
Access Agriculture: how sanitation and simple steps break the weevil cycle.
Access Agriculture: how farmers establish and care for weaver ant colonies.
A long field film on how anthracnose spreads and how farmers can cut losses.
Step-by-step pruning to keep trees low, open and productive.
Access Agriculture: grafting chosen varieties onto local rootstocks.

children.topic: ▶ Proper handling of mangoes at harvest
children.note: Access Agriculture: picking, de-sapping and handling to avoid damage.
Trusted sources for further study.
Indian varieties, spacing, manure schedule, flowering and yields.
Classic review of the disease, its economic impact and integrated control.
How ants affect pests, damage and yield across many studies.
Botany, history, varieties and world production.

nodeData.note: Oranges, tangerines (mandarins) and lemons are grafted trees that bear for decades. Organic success rests on clean nursery trees, the right rootstock, good drainage, conserved natural enemies and fast action against greening.

children.note: Citrus covers oranges, mandarins/tangerines, lemons, limes and grapefruit. All are grafted onto a rootstock chosen for the soil and disease risks.
Sweet orange (Citrus sinensis), mandarin or tangerine (C. reticulata), lemon (C. limon), lime and grapefruit are the main types. Many modern varieties are hybrids such as tangelos.

manas.q: What is the botanical name of the sweet orange?

children.note: Valencia and Washington Navel oranges, Minneola tangelo and the seedless Pixie tangerine are popular. Pixie growing has spread fast in Makueni and other dry Eastern counties.
Nagpur mandarin, Kinnow (Punjab), Coorg mandarin, Mosambi sweet orange and Kagzi acid lime are the best-known types. TNAU lists Coorg and Kodai oranges for the hill zones.
Citrus does not ripen further after picking; sugar and flavour stop developing once the fruit is cut. Pick only when it tastes ready.

manas.q: Do oranges ripen after harvest?

children.note: Citrus grows from sea level to cool highlands, but heat, altitude and drainage change fruit quality and disease.
Lowland heat gives sweet fruit but greenish peel; cool nights at higher altitude turn the peel orange. Mandarins in TNAU's hill zones grow at 500–1500 m.

manas.q: Why do oranges from hot lowlands often stay green when ripe?

children.note: Citrus roots die in waterlogged soil and Phytophthora thrives there. Choose deep, free-draining soil or plant on ridges.

manas.q: Which soil condition most favours Phytophthora in citrus?

children.note: TNAU recommends deep loams with pH 5.5–6.5 for mandarin; it also advises lime or dolomite every 2–3 years on acid hill soils.
Most serious citrus diseases arrive with the planting material. Clean trees on the right rootstock are the best investment a grower can make.
Buy from a certified nursery that raises budwood under insect-proof screens. A tree carrying greening or tristeza will never recover.

manas.q: Why must citrus nurseries be insect-screened?

children.note: A bud of the chosen variety is grafted onto a seedling rootstock. Keep the bud union well above the soil to avoid collar infection.
The rootstock gives disease tolerance, vigour and drought or salt tolerance.
The usual rootstock in Kenya and much of India: vigorous and drought-hardy, but prone to Phytophthora and gives larger, less sweet fruit.

manas.q: What is the most common citrus rootstock in Kenya?

children.note: Widely used in India and Brazil for its tolerance of drought and salt. It is sensitive to some graft-transmitted viroids.
Trifoliate orange and its hybrids (Carrizo/Troyer citrange, Swingle citrumelo) tolerate Phytophthora and tristeza but suffer in alkaline, chalky soils.

manas.q: Name a rootstock tolerant of Phytophthora root rot.

children.topic: Avoid sour orange where tristeza occurs
children.note: Sour orange gives good fruit and resists gummosis, but sweet orange on sour orange collapses when tristeza virus is present.
TNAU uses 6 × 6 m with 75 cm pits for mandarin. Fill pits with topsoil and well-rotted compost a few weeks before planting.
Citrus is a heavy feeder for nitrogen and potassium and often short of zinc, magnesium and manganese.
TNAU gives 10 kg FYM per mandarin tree in year 1, rising to 30 kg from year 6, applied in two splits. Organic growers meet the NPK part with compost, manure and legumes.

manas.q: How much FYM does TNAU suggest per mature mandarin tree?

children.note: Feeder roots lie under the outer canopy, so spread compost in a ring under the drip line, not against the trunk.

children.topic: Mulch, but not at the collar
children.note: Mulch keeps roots cool and moist, but keep it clear of the trunk; wet mulch at the collar invites gummosis.
Zinc lack gives small, narrow, mottled leaves; magnesium lack gives an inverted yellow V on older leaves. Organic standards allow trace-element salts when a test shows the need.

manas.q: What does magnesium deficiency look like on citrus leaves?

children.note: Sow cowpea, lablab or sunn hemp between rows and slash them for mulch, adding nitrogen and organic matter.
Microbes help roots take up nutrients; use them with compost.
Citrus roots have few root hairs and depend heavily on mycorrhizal fungi. TNAU advises 1 kg mycorrhiza inoculum per mature mandarin tree.

manas.q: Why does citrus benefit so much from mycorrhiza?

children.note: Mix with compost and apply into moist soil under the canopy after harvest. Keep apart from copper sprays.
Adding Trichoderma-enriched compost at planting helps protect young roots against soil pathogens.
Inoculation methods and how to see mycorrhiza working.
Citrus needs steady moisture for fruit set and size, but its roots hate wet feet.
Flowering, fruit set and fruit growth are the stages where drought causes fruit drop and small fruit.

manas.q: At which stages is water stress most harmful to citrus?

children.note: In the tropics, a dry spell followed by irrigation triggers a flush of flowers. Indian growers time this to choose the crop season (bahar).
Drip saves water and keeps the trunk dry. Never let water stand against the trunk, which favours gummosis.
Psyllids, false codling moth, scales, fruit flies and leaf miner are the main pests. Conserving natural enemies is the backbone of organic control.
Psyllids are tiny sap-sucking bugs that spread greening. Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri) and African citrus psyllid (Trioza erytreae) both occur in East Africa.
Young shoots twist and curl; African psyllid nymphs make pimple-like pits on leaves; Asian psyllid nymphs leave white waxy threads.

manas.q: What do African citrus psyllid nymphs do to leaves?

children.note: The Asian citrus psyllid was found in Tanzania in 2014–15 surveys and in Kenya soon after, raising the risk of the Asian form of greening.

manas.q: Which invasive citrus psyllid was recently found in Kenya?

children.note: Check new flushes weekly, prune off infested shoots, use yellow sticky traps, and spray neem or horticultural oil on flushes when psyllids are found.
The parasitic wasp Tamarixia radiata attacks Asian psyllid nymphs and has been released in Florida and California.
Psyllids, aphids, scales and mites in detail.
Thaumatotibia leucotreta, an African moth whose caterpillar bores into citrus, avocado and many other fruits.
A small hole with brown frass and a yellow-brown patch on the peel; infested fruit colours early and drops.

manas.q: What are the signs of false codling moth on an orange?

children.note: The EU treats FCM as a quarantine pest, so a single live larva can block a consignment. South Africa uses a systems approach to meet this.
Pick up and destroy dropped fruit twice a week, monitor with pheromone traps, and use mating disruption, the FCM granulovirus (CrleGV) and egg parasitoids.

manas.q: Name a virus used as a biopesticide against false codling moth.

children.note: Entomopathogenic nematodes from citrus orchards kill FCM larvae and pupae in the soil under trees.
Bt, viruses, pheromones and other caterpillar controls.
Red scale (armoured) and soft scales suck sap; soft scales and mealybugs make honeydew and sooty mould.
Crusty or waxy bumps on twigs, leaves and fruit, yellow spots under them, sticky leaves and black sooty mould.

manas.q: Which scale insects produce sticky honeydew?

children.note: Aphytis and other tiny wasps and ladybirds (Chilocorus) keep scales low when not killed by broad-spectrum sprays.
Ants farm soft scales and chase away their enemies. Sticky bands or barriers on trunks let natural enemies work.

manas.q: Why does controlling ants reduce scale problems?

children.note: Horticultural mineral oil, allowed in organic, smothers young scales. Aim at the crawler stage and avoid spraying in hot midday sun.
Fruit flies attack ripening fruit, especially mandarins; leaf miner larvae tunnel young leaves and open entry for canker.
Baits, lures and orchard sanitation.
Greening is the deadliest citrus disease; Phytophthora is the commonest killer of young and waterlogged trees.
Huanglongbing is caused by phloem bacteria (Candidatus Liberibacter species) spread by psyllids and infected budwood. There is no cure.
Blotchy, uneven yellow mottling not matching across the midrib, yellow shoots, small lopsided bitter fruit that stay green at the bottom, and aborted seeds.

manas.q: How does greening leaf mottle differ from nutrient deficiency?

children.note: Asian (Ca. L. asiaticus) is spread by the Asian psyllid; African (Ca. L. africanus) by the African citrus psyllid, which favours cool highlands.

manas.q: Which psyllid spreads African greening?

children.note: Plant clean nursery trees, control psyllids on new flushes, remove infected trees quickly and work with neighbours. Good nutrition and root health help trees cope.
Greening, canker and other bacterial diseases.
Water moulds (Phytophthora nicotianae, P. citrophthora) rot the bark at the collar and the feeder roots.
Gum oozing from cracked bark near the soil, dead brown bark under it, yellowing canopy and dieback; fruit near the ground gets brown rot.

manas.q: What is the first visible sign of citrus gummosis?

children.note: Use tolerant rootstocks, plant high with the bud union above soil, avoid wounds and water against the trunk, and improve drainage.
Scrape away diseased bark to healthy tissue and paint with Bordeaux paste; apply Trichoderma-enriched compost under the canopy. Biocontrol fungi have shown promise in trials.
Metalaxyl/mefenoxam and phosphonate fungicides used conventionally are not permitted under organic standards.

manas.q: Are phosphonates allowed for Phytophthora control in organic citrus?

children.note: Phytophthora and other root diseases.
Citrus tristeza virus spreads with aphids and budwood; trees on sour orange decline quickly. Use tolerant rootstocks and clean budwood.
How plant viruses spread and are managed.
Citrus black spot (a fungus) blemishes fruit and is an EU quarantine disease; citrus canker (a bacterium) causes raised corky spots. Copper, with limits, and sanitation help.
A clean, mulched basin and slashed ground cover between rows keep weeds in check.
Citrus feeder roots are near the surface, so deep hoeing damages them and opens the way for root rot. Mulch and hand-pull instead.

manas.q: Why should deep hoeing be avoided under citrus?

children.note: Slash grass or legumes between rows. Flowering cover also feeds the parasitoids and predators that control citrus pests.
Mulch, cover crops and mechanical weeding.
Good picking and handling keep citrus sound for weeks; rough handling causes rots and peel damage.
Harvest when the sugar-to-acid balance is right for the market, not by colour alone, since warm-area fruit stays green.
Cut the stem close to the fruit with clippers. Pulling tears the peel, and long stems puncture other fruit.

manas.q: Why should citrus be clipped rather than pulled?

children.note: Turgid fruit picked wet or early in the morning bruises easily, releasing peel oil that leaves dark spots. Pick dry fruit.
Pack in clean ventilated crates and keep cool. Synthetic post-harvest fungicides and waxes are not permitted in organic packing.
Citrus sells fresh and for juice. Export markets are strict on quarantine pests and residues.
Kenya imports many oranges, so local fresh-fruit and juice markets are open for good quality. Pixies sell well in Nairobi and Mombasa.
The EU sets strict rules for citrus imports on FCM, black spot and greening. Fruit must come from registered, inspected orchards.
Buyers check pesticide residues against limits. Organic fruit avoids synthetic residues but must still meet copper limits.
In Kenya, KEPHIS inspects and the Horticultural Crops Directorate registers exporters. In India, APEDA oversees exports and NPOP organic certification.
How to certify, alone or as a group.
Practical videos on citrus health and organic pest control.
University of Florida: what HLB is, how it spreads and why it matters.

children.topic: ▶ Scouting for the Asian citrus psyllid
children.note: Entomological Society of America: finding eggs, nymphs and adults on flush.
Kenyan report on biological options against FCM.
NSW Agriculture: beneficial insects that keep citrus pests down.
NSW Agriculture: monitoring and biological control of soft scale.
Citizen TV Smart Farm: a Kenyan orange grower's practices.
Trusted sources for further study.
Climate, spacing, manure schedule and mycorrhiza use for mandarin.
The first report of the Asian psyllid in Kenya and what it means for greening.
How soil and plant microbes may help citrus cope with greening.
Causes, vectors, symptoms and world spread of HLB.

nodeData.note: A field guide to growing arabica coffee organically, with a focus on Kenya: resistant varieties, shade, mulching and pulp compost, and organic answers to berry borer, Antestia, CBD and leaf rust.

children.note: Arabica coffee (Coffea arabica) is a self-pollinating evergreen shrub from the Ethiopian highlands; robusta (C. canephora) is a lowland species. Kenya grows almost only arabica, mostly on small farms organised in cooperatives.
Arabica grows at higher, cooler altitudes and gives the finer cup; robusta tolerates heat and lowlands, has more caffeine and a harsher taste. India grows both, Uganda mainly robusta.

manas.q: Which coffee species does Kenya mainly grow?

children.note: Tall Kenyan selections made by Scott Agricultural Laboratories in the 1930s. They give Kenya's famous bright, fruity cup, but both are susceptible to coffee berry disease and leaf rust.

manas.q: What is the main weakness of SL28 and SL34?

children.note: A compact hybrid released by Kenya's Coffee Research Institute in 1985, resistant to coffee berry disease and leaf rust. Its short stature allows closer spacing than the tall SL types.

manas.q: When was Ruiru 11 released and what does it resist?

children.note: A tall, true-breeding variety released in 2010, resistant to CBD and leaf rust, with a cup quality close to SL28. Seed can be saved from it, unlike the Ruiru 11 hybrid.

manas.q: Name the tall Kenyan variety released in 2010 that resists CBD and rust.

children.note: Old SL trees can be top-worked: Ruiru 11 or Batian scions are grafted onto new suckers, so the farmer keeps the old root system while gaining disease resistance. This sharply cuts the need for copper sprays.

manas.q: How can a farmer convert old SL28 trees to a resistant variety without uprooting?

children.note: India's Coffee Board and the Central Coffee Research Institute (Chikmagalur) breed arabica and robusta selections for Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu, mostly grown under two-tier shade.
Arabica needs mild temperatures, well-spread rain with a short dry spell to trigger flowering, and deep, well-drained, slightly acid soil rich in organic matter.
In Kenya arabica is grown roughly between 1,400 and 2,100 m around Mt Kenya, the Aberdares, Kisii, Mt Elgon and Kericho/Nandi. Heat above about 30 °C stresses arabica and favours berry borer.

manas.q: Why is heat bad for arabica beyond plant stress?

children.note: Kenya's two rainy seasons give two flowerings and so a main and a fly crop. Flowers open a week or so after rain that ends a dry spell.
Deep red volcanic soils, slightly acid, well drained and full of organic matter suit coffee best. Waterlogged or shallow soils lead to root rots and dieback.
Warming is pushing arabica's ideal zone uphill and lets berry borer breed more often; shade trees are the main on-farm adaptation suggested by East African studies.
A coffee farm stays productive for decades, so time spent on clean seedlings, good holes and shade planning pays back for years.
Buy seed or seedlings of Ruiru 11 or Batian from certified sources (Coffee Research Institute or licensed nurseries). Home-raised Ruiru 11 seed does not breed true.

manas.q: Why should Ruiru 11 seed not be saved on-farm?

children.note: Raise seedlings in polybags of topsoil, sand and well-matured compost, under 50% shade, with clean water. Mycorrhiza and Trichoderma added to the mix give healthier roots.
Dig holes well ahead of the rains, keep topsoil and subsoil apart, and refill with topsoil mixed with plenty of mature manure or compost. Plant at the start of the long rains.
Plant shade trees such as Grevillea, Cordia africana or Albizia before or with the coffee, so they are useful when the bushes start bearing.
On slopes make terraces or contour bunds and grass strips (such as Napier) before planting to stop erosion of the topsoil.

Coffee removes nitrogen and potassium in the largest amounts, mostly in cherries and prunings. An organic plan returns these through compost, pulp, prunings, manure and legumes, with biofertilizers to unlock soil nutrients.
Each crop exports N, K, P, Ca and Mg in the cherries. Leaves and prunings left in the field recycle a large share; pulp sent back from the factory returns much of the rest.

manas.q: Which two nutrients does coffee remove in the largest amounts?

children.note: Pale yellow older leaves suggest nitrogen shortage; scorched leaf edges and poor berry filling suggest potassium; small, narrow, crowded leaves at shoot tips suggest zinc.
Pulp from wet processing is rich in potassium and organic matter. Compost it in heaps mixed with manure and dry material, turning until it no longer smells sour, before spreading under bushes.

manas.q: Which nutrient is coffee pulp especially rich in?

children.note: Earthworms such as Eudrilus eugeniae can turn coffee pulp into a fine vermicompost; trials in Colombia and India found it a better product than simple turned piles.

links.label: 📄 Source: Biology and Fertility of Soils 1996

children.note: Spread well-rotted cattle or goat manure in a ring under the drip line at the start of the rains, then cover with mulch. Never pile fresh manure against the stem.
Leguminous shade trees, Desmodium or beans between young rows, and lopped Calliandra or Leucaena leaves add nitrogen and organic matter.

Nursery: mycorrhiza and Trichoderma in the potting mix. Planting: the same in the hole with compost. Mature bushes: Azotobacter or Azospirillum, PSB and KMB mixed into compost and applied at the onset of rains.

manas.q: Which biofertilizers suit the coffee nursery mix?

children.note: Very acid soils can be corrected with agricultural lime or dolomite, which are allowed in organic farming; rock phosphate supplies slow phosphorus. Base decisions on a soil test.
Synthetic fertilizers such as CAN, urea or NPK compounds are not permitted on certified organic coffee.
Coffee roots are shallow, so keeping the topsoil cool and moist through the dry season decides next year's crop.
A thick mulch of dry grass, maize stover or prunings keeps soil moist and cool, feeds soil life and smothers weeds. Keep it a hand's width away from the stem.

manas.q: Why keep mulch away from the coffee stem?

children.note: Moderate shade buffers heat, slows weeds and drops leaf litter. Too much shade lowers yield and keeps leaves wet, so lop shade trees before the rains.

manas.q: What happens when coffee is over-shaded?

children.note: A Brazilian study found shade trees changed soil nutrients and soil fauna more strongly on organic than on conventional coffee farms.

links.label: 📄 Source: Science of the Total Environment 2019

children.note: In robusta farms of Kodagu, India, farms with more kinds of shade trees had higher yields, bigger beans and less berry borer than farms dominated by one tree species.

manas.q: What did the Kodagu study find about diverse shade?

children.note: Where irrigation exists, a single watering after a long dry spell can produce an even flowering; drip and basin irrigation save water.
Pruning keeps bushes open, light and productive, and removes the wood where pests and diseases build up.
Kenyan farmers train SL and Batian bushes on one to three upright stems (capped multiple-stem system); remove excess suckers regularly.
Remove dead, crossing and inward-growing branches after harvest so light and air reach the centre; this cuts rust, CBD and berry borer habitat.

manas.q: How does pruning help against coffee diseases?

children.note: Unproductive bushes can be cut low to regrow new stems; plan it after harvest and keep the stumps mulched and fed.
The pests that matter most in Kenya are the coffee berry borer, Antestia bugs, leaf miners, thrips, mealybugs, scales and stem borers.
Hypothenemus hampei is a tiny black beetle, the world's worst coffee pest. The female bores a hole at the tip (navel) of the berry and breeds inside the bean.

manas.q: Where on the berry does the berry borer enter?

children.note: A neat pinhole at the berry tip, sometimes with fine dust; bored green berries drop, and bored beans are hollowed and lose weight and grade.
The beetle develops faster in warm conditions, so it is spreading to higher coffee zones as temperatures rise.
Clean harvesting (pick all ripe, overripe and fallen berries; strip at season end), Beauveria bassiana sprays, alcohol-baited traps and African parasitoid wasps. Shade with diverse trees helps.

manas.q: What is the key cultural control for berry borer?

children.note: Opens the beetles map for biology and organic control of borers and weevils.
Antestiopsis species are shield bugs with orange, black and white markings. They suck buds, flowers and green berries.

manas.q: What do Antestia bugs look like?

children.note: Flower buds blacken and drop, berries fall, beans inside show zebra-like brown streaks, and shoots become bushy with many small branches (fan branching).
Antestia feeding is linked to 'potato taste' defect in East African coffee, which spoils whole lots at cupping.

manas.q: Which cup defect is linked to Antestia bugs?

children.note: Unlike most coffee pests, Antestia is most numerous at higher, cooler elevations and in the cool dry season.
Prune to open the bush, hand-pick and shake bugs onto a sheet early in the morning, and use pyrethrum (natural, organic-allowed) only where counts are high.
Opens the sucking pests map: bugs, mealybugs, scales, thrips and mites.

Leaf miner caterpillars make brown blotch mines on upper leaves; thrips cause silvery, scarred leaves in hot dry spells. Natural enemies usually keep both in check if broad-spectrum sprays are avoided.
These suck sap at berry clusters and shoots and are farmed by ants for honeydew. Band stems with sticky grease to keep ants off, and natural enemies will usually clean them up.
A longhorn beetle larva rings the bark near the ground and tunnels in the stem, often killing young bushes. Check stems for frass, kill larvae with a wire and keep the base clean.
Coffee berry disease and leaf rust are the two big fungal diseases in Kenya; root rots and wilt matter locally.
Colletotrichum kahawae attacks green, expanding berries. It is found only in Africa and can destroy most of a crop on susceptible varieties in wet years.

manas.q: Which coffee stage does CBD attack?

children.note: Small dark sunken spots on green berries that spread and blacken the berry; dead berries stay mummified on the branch and carry spores to the next season.
Spores splash in rain and drip from mummified berries and bark; cool wet weather during berry expansion is the danger period, worst at high altitude.
In Cameroon, shaded coffee had less CBD than coffee in full sun; shade changed the microclimate rather than the berries' own susceptibility.

manas.q: How does shade reduce CBD?

children.note: Plant Ruiru 11 or Batian or graft them; prune and remove mummified berries; time copper sprays (allowed with limits) to the main berry expansion rains.
Opens the blights map with CBD and other wet-weather diseases.
Hemileia vastatrix causes yellow-orange powdery spots on the underside of leaves and heavy leaf fall; it is worse at lower, warmer altitudes.

manas.q: Where on the leaf is the orange rust powder?

children.note: Resistant varieties first; then balanced organic feeding, open pruning, moderate shade and copper protectant sprays before the rains.
In a Mexican shaded farm, outbreaks of the fungus Lecanicillium lecanii on green scales were followed a year later by lower rust levels.
Opens the mildews and rusts map.

Armillaria root rot kills bushes planted on land cleared from forest; coffee wilt (Fusarium xylarioides) is serious in Uganda and DRC. Remove dead bushes with their roots and do not move planting material from wilt areas.
Root-knot and lesion nematodes cause stunting and yellowing, worst in nurseries on reused soil. Use clean nursery soil and compost-rich planting holes.
Weeds compete hardest with young coffee and in dry spells, especially couch grass and other perennial grasses.
Mulch, leguminous covers and shade keep weeds down; slash or hand-weed rings around young bushes.
Deep hoeing cuts coffee's shallow feeding roots; shallow weeding or slashing is safer. Herbicides are not allowed in organic coffee.

manas.q: Why avoid deep hoeing under coffee?

children.note: Quality is made at picking and at the factory: only ripe red cherries, processed the same day, give Kenya's top grades.
Pick only fully ripe red cherries every one to two weeks; sort out green, dry and bored berries before delivery.

manas.q: Which cherries should be picked for top quality?

children.note: Kenyan factories pulp, ferment, wash, soak and sun-dry parchment on raised tables. Clean water and careful drying protect the cup.
Pulp should go back to farms as compost, and wastewater should settle in lagoons or soak pits, not run into rivers, where it kills aquatic life.
Store dry parchment in clean bags on pallets, away from smoke, fuel and chemicals that taint coffee.
Kenyan coffee is sold through the Nairobi Coffee Exchange or by direct sales; organic and other certifications can open specialty markets.
About 70% of Kenyan coffee comes from smallholders, mostly through cooperative factories; production has fallen from its 1980s peak.
Exports must meet the buyer's standard (EU organic, USDA NOP, or Japan's JAS); group certification with an internal control system lets cooperatives certify many smallholders together.
Importing countries set maximum residue limits on coffee; organic lots are tested and any synthetic pesticide residue can cost the certificate.
Selected videos from FAO, extension services, coffee boards and an experienced Kenyan grower.
FAO — farmer methods to control berry borer without the banned insecticide.

nodeData.note: A field guide to growing tea organically, focused on Kenyan smallholders (KTDA) with notes from India: clones, pruning and plucking, organic nutrition that stops soil acidification, biofertilizers, and organic control of mites and root rots.

children.note: Tea (Camellia sinensis) is an evergreen shrub kept as a flat-topped bush and plucked for its young shoots. Kenya, India, China and Sri Lanka are leading producers; Kenya is among the top black-tea exporters.
The China type (var. sinensis) is small-leaved and cold-tolerant; the Assam type (var. assamica) is large-leaved and high-yielding. Kenyan clones are mostly Assam-type.

manas.q: Which tea type are most Kenyan clones based on?

children.note: Tea came to Limuru in 1903 and estates began in 1924. Most Kenyan tea is CTC black tea for blends, plus some orthodox, green and purple tea.

manas.q: Where and when was tea first planted in Kenya?

children.note: The Kenya Tea Development Agency serves over half a million smallholders with extension, leaf collection, factories and marketing; they produce more than 60% of Kenya's tea.

manas.q: Roughly what share of Kenyan tea do KTDA smallholders produce?

children.note: The Tea Research Institute (KALRO-TRI, Kericho; formerly TRFK) has released many clones for yield, quality and drought tolerance, including purple-leaved tea rich in anthocyanins.

manas.q: Which institute breeds Kenyan tea clones?

children.note: Tocklai Tea Research Institute (Assam) and UPASI (south India) release clones and guidance; Darjeeling, Assam and the Nilgiris have certified organic gardens.
Tea needs plenty of well-spread rain, mild temperatures and deep, well-drained, strongly acid soil.
Kenya's tea zones on both sides of the Rift Valley receive about 1,200–1,400 mm of well-distributed rain on deep red volcanic soils at high altitude.
Tea grows best at soil pH about 4.5–5.5; in a Chinese national survey almost half of tea soils had fallen below 4.5, too acid for good growth.

manas.q: What soil pH range is best for tea?

links.label: 📄 Source: Science of the Total Environment 2020

children.note: Heavy nitrogen fertilizer is the main cause of acidification in tea gardens; long-term trials show pH falling as N doses rise.

manas.q: What is the main cause of soil acidification in tea gardens?

children.note: The same Chinese survey found no significant acidification on organic tea plantations, unlike gardens on chemical fertilizer.

links.label: 📄 Source: Science of the Total Environment 2020

children.note: Ground frost in high valleys and long dry spells in the east of the Rift scorch shoots; shade trees, mulch and drought-tolerant clones reduce damage.
Tea lives for many decades, so clean land, good cuttings and a strong first frame decide the garden's future.
Old tree stumps and roots carry Armillaria root rot. Ring-bark trees a year or more before felling and remove stumps and large roots before planting.

manas.q: Why ring-bark trees before clearing land for tea?

children.note: Tea is propagated from one-leaf, one-node cuttings of a chosen clone, rooted in sleeves of acid subsoil under shade and high humidity for several months.

manas.q: How are tea plants usually propagated?

children.note: Use acid, weed-free subsoil for rooting; avoid lime, ash and fresh manure, which raise pH and burn cuttings. Clean soil avoids nematodes.
Mycorrhizal fungi changed root system architecture and boosted growth of tea cuttings in pot trials, so adding AMF inoculum to nursery soil is promising.
Plant hardened plants at the start of the rains in holes enriched with mature compost; contour rows and grass strips protect slopes from erosion.
Young plants are pegged or tipped to form a wide, low frame that becomes the flat plucking table.
Tea removes a lot of nitrogen in every flush of plucked shoots. Organic gardens return it through compost, manure, prunings, oil cakes and legumes, and keep the soil from acidifying.
Every plucking round carries away young shoots rich in nitrogen and potassium, so nitrogen is the nutrient most often limiting tea yields.

manas.q: Which nutrient most often limits tea yield?

children.note: Nitrogen: pale small leaves and slow flushing. Potassium: scorched leaf margins and dieback. Magnesium: yellow patches between veins on mature leaves. Zinc: small, narrow, sickle-shaped leaves.
Pruning litter is a huge nutrient bank; leaving it as mulch returns nutrients and organic matter instead of burning or selling it as firewood.

manas.q: Why should tea prunings stay in the garden?

children.note: Apply mature compost or cattle manure between rows at the start of the rains and cover with mulch. In a 4-year trial organic-only plots kept pH 5.1–5.3 while chemical plots fell below 3.
Seed cakes such as rapeseed, neem or castor cake are concentrated organic N sources; rapeseed cake buffered acidification and cut N runoff in a Chinese tea trial.

links.label: 📄 Source: Science of the Total Environment 2021

children.note: Tea gardens managed long-term with organic fertilizer had better rhizosphere soil properties than those on chemical fertilizer in a long-term field study.
Leguminous shade and hedge trees and cover crops in young tea add nitrogen and leaf litter; lop them regularly so they do not over-shade.

manas.q: Name one way legumes add N to a tea garden.

children.note: Nursery: mycorrhiza and Trichoderma in the sleeve soil. Field: Azospirillum, a P solubiliser, mycorrhiza and a K mobiliser mixed with compost after pruning and at the onset of rains.

manas.q: Which biofertilizer package does TNAU suggest for tea?

children.note: Only where pH has fallen far below 4.5 should small doses of dolomite be used, guided by a soil test; liming tea like a maize field harms it.
Synthetic NPK fertilizers such as the compound blends supplied to many smallholders are not permitted on certified organic tea.
Tea is mostly rain-fed; keeping soil covered and partly shaded carries bushes through dry spells.
Mulch young tea heavily with grass or prunings to keep soil cool and moist and to stop erosion until the canopy closes.

manas.q: Why mulch young tea?

children.note: Scattered shade trees such as Grevillea reduce heat and drought stress, add leaf litter and give firewood and timber income.
Where available, irrigation of nurseries and young tea in the dry season prevents losses; most mature smallholder tea is rain-fed.
Pruning keeps the bush at a comfortable plucking height and renews the frame; regular plucking keeps it flushing.
Over years the plucking table rises and gets knotty and less productive; pruning brings it down and renews vigorous shoots.

manas.q: Why do tea bushes need periodic pruning?

children.note: Kenyan bushes are usually pruned every few years, at the end of the rains or in a cool period, never during drought stress.
Leaving a few branches unpruned ('lungs') helps the bush recover faster, especially in drier areas.

manas.q: What are the lung branches in tea pruning?

children.note: New shoots are tipped at an even height to form a level plucking table before regular plucking resumes.
Pluck two leaves and a bud at regular rounds of about one to two weeks; coarse plucking lowers quality and price.

manas.q: What is the standard fine plucking unit for tea?

children.note: Mites, thrips and sucking bugs are the main tea pests; most are kept down by natural enemies when broad-spectrum sprays are avoided.
Oligonychus coffeae turns mature leaves bronze-red on the upper surface in hot dry weather, with fine webbing. Predatory mites and rains bring it down.

manas.q: What weather favours red spider mite in tea?

children.note: Keep bushes well fed and mulched, avoid dust on leaves, conserve predatory mites and ladybirds, and use sulphur or neem only on hot spots.
Opens the sucking pests map: mites, thrips, aphids and bugs.
Tiny insects that scar young leaves, leaving silvery or brown streaks on both sides of the midrib, worst in dry spells. Regular plucking removes many eggs and larvae.
Helopeltis species (a major pest in India) suck young shoots, leaving dark sunken spots that make shoots shrivel. Prune and pluck infested shoots and use neem or Beauveria where severe.
Termites attack drought-stressed or wounded bushes; lesion and root-knot nematodes stunt young tea. Use clean nursery soil and compost-rich planting holes.
Natural enemies, entomopathogenic fungi and botanicals form the base of pest control in organic tea; India's tea research body promotes them widely.
Root rots are the main killers in Kenyan tea; in Asia the leaf disease blister blight is the biggest threat.
Armillaria fungi spread from old forest stumps along roots and kill bushes in patches. White fan-shaped fungal sheets lie under the bark at the collar.

manas.q: What sign under the bark identifies Armillaria root rot?

children.note: Dig out dead bushes with all roots and stumps; leave the ground fallow or under grass before replanting; ring-bark trees long before clearing.

manas.q: What must be removed when a tea bush dies of Armillaria?

children.note: Pseudomonas strains induced defence enzymes in tea against brown root rot and charcoal stump rot in experiments; Trichoderma is also used in compost around replants.
Opens the root rots map.
A wood-decaying fungus in Kenyan tea that enters through pruning cuts and stressed stems; branches die back. Prune cleanly in good weather and keep bushes vigorous.
Exobasidium vexans makes pale, translucent spots on young leaves that bulge into white blisters underneath; it is serious in India and Sri Lanka in misty monsoon weather.

manas.q: Which tea disease causes white blisters under young leaves?

children.note: Sunlight, especially its UV-B part, reduces blister blight; lopping shade during the monsoon helps.
Weekly foliar Pseudomonas fluorescens reduced blister blight almost as well as a chemical fungicide in Indian field trials; copper is the organic fallback.

manas.q: Which bacterium controlled blister blight in Indian tea trials?

children.note: A leaf-surface bacterium from tea also suppressed grey and blister blight in field tests, an area still under research.
Opens the blights map.
Weeds compete hardest in young tea before the canopy closes; mature tea shades most weeds out.
Mulch and careful hand weeding or slashing in young tea; avoid deep digging that cuts feeder roots and causes erosion.
Low cover crops or Guatemala grass mulch between young rows hold soil; herbicides are not allowed in organic tea.

manas.q: Are herbicides allowed in organic tea?

children.note: Green leaf starts to wilt and lose quality the moment it is plucked, so care in handling decides price.
Carry leaf in clean, airy baskets, keep it in shade and deliver to the buying centre quickly; never pack it in plastic or let it heat up.

manas.q: Why should plucked tea leaf never be packed tightly in plastic?

children.note: Factories wither, cut (CTC) or roll, ferment, dry and grade the leaf; about 4 kg of green leaf makes 1 kg of made tea.

manas.q: About how much green leaf makes 1 kg of made tea?

children.note: Smoke from firewood dryers and plastics can leave contaminants that exceed buyer limits; organic factories must keep organic leaf separate.
Most Kenyan tea is sold at the Mombasa auction; organic, Rainforest Alliance and Fairtrade lots reach specialty buyers.
A garden must be managed organically for a conversion period before its tea can be sold as organic; group certification lets smallholders certify together.
The EU and other importers set strict maximum residue limits for tea, which is brewed and drunk without washing; organic leaf is tested for residues.

manas.q: Why are residue limits on tea especially strict?

children.note: Orthodox, green, white and purple teas from Kenya earn premiums in niche markets, often linked to organic certification.
